title: Harper settling in at first for Phillies
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Harper settling in at first for Phillies

 February 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1090
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Bryce Harper is getting settled in as full-time first baseman for the Philadelphia Phillies.Harper hit a hard single in his first spring training at-bat Wednesday, but the two-time NL MVP also flashed some leather at first base in a 7-7 tie against Atlanta. Harper made a diving catch on Jarred Kelenic's grounder in the first inning, and started nifty 3-6-3 on a 105.3 mph grounder by Kelenic in the third.
"Both of them were real good," Phillies manager Rob Thomson said. "He looks very comfortable and he's improving every day."
Harper had Tommy John surgery in November 2022 and made his season debut last May 2 as a designated hitter. An outfielder the previous 11 seasons, his return to the field July 21 was at first base, where he started 36 times in the regular season and 13 in the playoffs.
"The sky's the limit for me because he's athletic," Thomson said. "He's calm, poised. A lot of a lot of good things can happen."
Former Phillies first baseman Rhys Hoskins tore his left ACL in a spring training game last March, and left in free agency after the season.
MUNCY HITBefore Japanese sensation Yoshinobu Yamamoto threw the first pitch in an impressive spring training debut for the Dodgers against World Series champion Texas, Los Angeles third baseman Max Muncy got hit by a pitch on his left hand in the top of the first inning.
Manager Dave Roberts said the ball hit Muncy on the knuckle of his ring finger and that the veteran was getting tests.
"I'm hopeful that it's not going to be too serious," Roberts said.
After getting hit by left-hander Cody Bradford, Muncy stayed in the game to play defense, and was replaced in the fourth inning by Austin Gauthier before his second at-bat. A mainstay in the middle of the Dodgers order the past six seasons, Muncy hit 36 homers and had 105 RBIs last year.
Yamamoto struck out three batters over two scoreless innings.
COUNSELL VS. BREWERSThere was a mix of cheers and boos when new Chicago Cubs manager Craig Counsell returned to his old spring training home for the first time.
The Cubs won 6-1 on the road Wednesday against the Milwaukee Brewers, the NL Central rival Counsell managed the past nine seasons.
"It's weird seeing him in those colors, but that's what reality is right now," said new Brewers manager Pat Murphy, who was on Counsell's staff the past eight years.
Brewers shortstop Willy Adames went across the field to hug Counsell before the game.
Budget-conscious Milwaukee won three NL Central titles and made five playoff appearances the past six years before Counsell's contract expired. The Cubs lured him away with a five-year contract worth more than $40 million that made him the highest-paid manager the majors.
SONNY OPENERSonny Gray will be the first Cardinals pitcher since Kyle Lohse in 2008 to make his debut for the Cardinals with a start on opening day.
"I don't take that lightly at all," said Gray, the veteran right-hander who signed a $75 million, three-year deal in November. "I appreciate the opportunity and what that shows."
Gray finished second in the AL Cy Young Award voting last season, when he was 8-8 with a 2.79 ERA in 32 starts for Minnesota. The Cardinals also added former All-Stars Kyle Gibson and Lance Lynn to their rotation in free agency.
St. Louis, coming off its first losing season since 2007, opens March 28 on the road against Shohei Ohtani and the Dodgers.
TOP PICK SKENES TO PITCH THURSDAYPittsburgh pitching prospect Paul Skenes, the top pick in last year's amateur draft, is to make his spring training debut on Thursday when the Pirates face Baltimore and Jackson Holliday, the No. 1 selection last summer.
The 21-year-old Skenes had a 5.40 ERA with 10 strikeouts and two walks in 6 2/3 innings in limited action in the minors after signing a record $9.2 million bonus to join Pittsburgh.
While the Pirates have a couple of open spots in their starting rotation, it's likely the hard-throwing Skenes will begin his first full season as a professional in the minors. He was 12-2 with a 1.69 ERA and 209 strikeouts in 122 2/3 innings last spring while playing for national champion LSU.
PEN PROBLEMThe Cleveland Guardians are shutting down reliever Trevor Stephan for three weeks with a deep bruise in his right elbow. Stephan, who appeared in 71 games last season, experienced soreness during a recent training session in Goodyear, Arizona. An MRI revealed the bruising.
Manager Stephen Vogt said Stephan has no structural or ligament issues.
The 28-year-old Stephan went 7-7 with a 4.06 ERA last season.
TJ AGAIN FOR THOMPSONNationals right-hander Mason Thompson will undergo Tommy John surgery for the second time.
Thompson first had the ligament replacement surgery when he was in high school. Now 26 and coming off 51 appearances for the Nationals last season, he felt a pop in his elbow at the start of spring training two weeks ago.
Manager Dave Martinez said Thompson will have the surgery on Friday.
GIANTS INJURIES
Giants right-hander Tristan Beck returned to San Francisco to see doctors after dealing with lingering soreness in his right hander.
"He's kind of been pitching through it a bit," San Francisco manager Bob Melvin said. "It just got to a point where we want to find out exactly what it is."
Beck made his big league debut last season by going 3-3 with a 3.92 ERA in 33 games for the Giants. While he started only three of those games, he is expected to be part of their rotation this year.
Meanwhile, Giants outfielder Mike Yastrzemski made his spring debut Wednesday going 0 for 2 with a walk in their 7-4 loss to Oakland. There are no restrictions at the plate even though he is still building up his throwing from a left shoulder issue that developed during offseason workouts.
SOME CLAIMS AND MOVES
— The Yankees claimed infielder Jahmai Jones off waivers from the Brewers. Infielder Jordan Groshans was designated for assignment to make room on New York's 40-man roster.
— Sam Hilliard is back with Colorado after being claimed the outfielder off waivers from Baltimore. The Rockies cleared a spot on their 40-man roster by putting right-hander Antonio Senzatela on the 60-day injured list.
Hilliard played 214 games with the Rockies from 2019-22 before getting traded to Atlanta. He played 40 games with the Braves last season before Baltimore claimed him off waivers in November.
— San Diego agreed to a minor league contract with 31-year-old outfielder Tim Locastro, who hit .232 with two homers and three RBIs and six stolen bases in 43 games and 67 plate appearances with the New York Mets last year.

title: Bucs ride post play, down NC
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Bucs ride post play, down NC

 February 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 691
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — There have been seasons when Kent Island High's girls basketball team has beaten opponents from long distance.That hasn't been the Bucs' most common thread to victory this season.
The one-two inside scoring punch of Sydney Riska and Makayla Kropfelder combined for 27 points, and Kent Island went on a 13-0 first-half scoring run Wednesday night to gain separation in an eventual 46-37 victory over North Caroline in a Class 2A East Region II quarterfinal.
The defending region champion, fourth-seeded Kent Island (18-3) advances to Friday's semifinal at top-seeded Wicomico (21-0). Second-seeded Queen Anne's (19-2) hosts No. 3 Parkside (18-3) in Friday's other semifinal.
"We used to be a three-point team and now we're a post team," Bucs head coach David Plumer said. "It's no secret. Everybody who watches film on us will know. But the post-play is getting better. Makayla and Sydney did great tonight. They can complement everybody else. We got the ball inside. We're a little bigger than them and we knew that."
North Caroline (14-7), which came in having won nine of its last 11, took a 6-4 lead a little over 3 minutes into the game, when Chloe Escoe (team-high 14 points) hit the second of her four 3-pointers. But Riska (game-high 17 points) scored on a put-back with 3:09 left in the first quarter to start the Buccaneers on a decisive 13-0 streak.
"We started off moving the ball early," North Caroline head coach A.J. Jackson said. "We had some good offensive possessions, but then we had a drought there where we got sort of undisciplined tonight, and that ended up hurting us later in the game."
The Bulldogs went 9 minutes without a field goal before Ashley Kercheval got behind the defense for a layup with 3:49 left in the first half, cutting Kent Island's lead to 20-8. Riska hit a pair of baskets during the run and Kropfelder (10 points) made a three-point play.
"We knew this was going to be a post-play game," said Riska, who finished with 13 rebounds for her 17th double-double of the season. "So just getting the ball down to me and Makayla, and then just getting the shots up. Obviously we didn't do well from the three-point line, but we did work well in the paint. The outside shots weren't falling for me but I worked inside to get it done."
As did Kropfelder.
"Just trying to make the best plays for my team," the sophomore center said. "If I'm not there, if there's too many defenders, pass it. I missed a couple opportunities but I just need to work on that personally."
Lacy Dauses hit a cutting Riska for a layup and a 23-10 halftime lead. Riska and Kropfelder then teamed to score all the points in a 6-0 burst to open the third quarter, expanding Kent Island's lead to 29-10 less than 3 minutes into the period.
But the Bulldogs outscored the Bucs, 14-4, over the remaining 4:52 of the third quarter to pull within 33-24 entering the fourth quarter.
Kent Island regained its double-digit lead with Lilli Dauses converting a pair of free throws and Kropfelder scoring off a Riska assist for a 37-24 cushion.
"Credit to their bigs," Jackson said. "Second-chance shots, they really battled down there. And the effort on defense, especially when we made a little run there in the fourth quarter. Like hustling, not giving up. That team is well coached. Credit to Plumer."
North Caroline again cut its deficit to under 10 with 5 minutes remaining when Escoe drilled another 3-pointer and Malayah Phillips scored on a layup to make it 37-29. But Kent Island twice worked the ball inside to Riska, who was fouled and hit four consecutive free throws to make it 41-29 midway through the final period.
The Bulldogs wouldn't get any closer than eight the remainder of the game, as their small runs were countered by the Bucs.
"It's always been a little bit of a dogfight," Kent Island guard Caroline Cavanaugh said. "We go in there, we get a lead, they come back. We just need to be a little more consistent with our defense and our offense. They played really well. We just played better this game."

title: TIME TRIALS

TIME TRIALS

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports

 CENTREVILLE — Giuseppe Mellinger needed a late block.Tremaine Jackson needed an extra minute.
And Scottie Ford. Well, he needed more time than either one of them.
No matter the time frame, Jackson, Ford and Mellinger each finished with the same result Saturday night at Queen Anne's County High, winning their respective weight classes at the Class 2A-1A East Regional wrestling championships.
"He's been one of our elite wrestlers for three years now," Queen Anne's head coach David Stricker said of Jackson, who with his 5-3 overtime victory against Rising Sun's Xzavier Brown in the 126-pound final earned his 99th career win. "Tremaine, he's just so quick. And his power has really come along this year. When he gets in on a leg it's really hard to fend off."
Saturday's region final was the third time Jackson and Brown faced off this season. Brown pieced together an 8-3 decision at the Westminster Duals in late December, then earned a 3-1 overtime win when the two met in the 2A-1A East Regional Duals earlier this month. Their third encounter would also take longer than six minutes.
"They've been wrestling each other since youth, so they've known each other really well," Stricker said. "I'm not surprised it went that far."
A senior, Jackson (35-3) scored a first-period takedown, but Brown escaped with 44 seconds left in the period to make it 2-1 after one. Brown (35-8) rode Jackson through a scoreless second period, and hit a reversal 11 seconds into the third period for a 3-2 lead. Jackson then got an escape off a restart with 15 seconds left in the third to forge a 3-3 tie, sending the match into a 1-minute overtime.
"It's obviously been a bit harder because they've been training him, trying to study my style, his coaches," Jackson said. "They obviously know me very well, the good moves I do. So yeah, it definitely was a lot more difficult than the other times wrestling him."
Brown got in a single-leg shot in the overtime, but Jackson blocked, spun and earned the takedown for the 5-3 sudden victory.
"My last match at the high school, and what was going through my head was, I can't lose," said Jackson, whose second regional title came five days after winning his third Bayside Conference crown. "I feel great. I put in the work. I think I've got a good shot of getting in the state finals."
Ford also had a familiar opponent in his 138-pound final — Parkside junior Rocco Tully — who the Kent County sophomore decisioned 6-0 in the Bayside championship five days earlier.
"I knew it was going to be tougher," said Ford, who coupled two takedowns with a reversal for Monday's 6-0 victory. "Every time you wrestle somebody it feels like it gets tougher and tougher. They always learn from it. I was nervous. I would have much rather faced somebody else I hadn't seen before."
After a scoreless first period, Ford (37-1) hit a switch off bottom for a reversal with 35 seconds left in the second period for a 2-0 lead. Tully (35-9) scored a takedown with 44 seconds to go in the third and rode Ford the rest of the period, forcing overtime.
Neither wrestler scored in the 1-minute overtime. Starting on top, Ford rode Tully through the first 30-second sudden-victory period. Less than two seconds into the second 30-second period, Ford reversed Tully and rode out the remainder of the period on top for the 4-2 win.
"I knew I had a good switch on him because on Monday I had a nice switch," Ford said. "He knows how to throw legs, so he's really tough on top, but I knew I could get out. I just beat him off the whistle."
Something that did not surprise Kent County head coach Chris Yiannakis.
"He's been on that switch," Yiannakis said of Ford. "That's one of his number one escapes from bottom. Most people can't stop it. It's so fast. Rocco did stop it in the first couple of periods though. He just wore him down by the final (period) and he couldn't stop it."
The 175-pound final was yet another Bayside rematch, as Mellinger (36-5) clashed with Parkside's Canaan Mapp (24-8) for the third time this season.
"The first time we wrestled he actually was more aggressive," said Mellinger, who defeated Mapp via a 12-4 major decision during the dual-meet season. "He would actually tie up with me and stuff. So that allowed me to work my offense. The second time, at Baysides (a 7-2 Mellinger win), he would run around, he kept moving, but I got a few takedowns there.
"This time, because I think his coaches were telling him how to make some good adjustments, he wasn't tying up," Mellinger continued. "He was keeping me at a distance. He would try to work in some shots, I would try to work in mine. But we both got a good shot defense. And then when we're so far apart, it's hard to score points."
Mellinger got a double-leg takedown 54 seconds into the match, but Mapp escaped 11 seconds later, making it 2-1 heading into the second. Mapp escaped five seconds into he second period to tie the match.
It remained that way until 18 seconds into the third, when Mellinger, starting on bottom, escaped to take a 3-2 lead. Mellinger blocked a shot midway through the period before a neutral restart with 41 seconds left. Mellinger got in a shot, but Mapp countered with a shot with less than 20 seconds left. The Kent Island senior, who was named the Bayside Conference's defensive player of the year in football for 2023, could not be taken down though, hanging on for the 3-2 win.
"I started getting a little nervous at the end when I took a shot and then he re-shot and got in on my leg with like 15 seconds left," Mellinger said. "And I was able to defend that because if he had gotten that and I didn't get up in time, that would have been the match."
It was Mellinger's first regional title.
"It's nice to win, said Mellinger, whose younger sister Lilliana won the 120-pound title at Friday night's girls 2A-1A East Regional. "My sister and I, we're both Bayside champions. Now, we're both regional champions. Now, we're both competing for a state title. That's cool. It's a lot of fun."
Said Kent Island head coach Tommy Sitar of Mellinger, "He had another great tournament. He worked really well in his matches leading up to the final, and fortunately got the win in the final. It's hard to beat a wrestler three times in a season. It's a good feat."
Kent Island seniors Greg Couch (132) and Cody Sandefer (144) each took runner-up honors, and seniors Brandon Adler (157) and Nick Morey (190) each won their consolation final to place third.
The top four in each weight class advance to this year's state tournament, which begins Thursday at the Show Place Arena in Upper Marlboro and concludes Saturday.
Stephen Decatur and Rising Sun each advanced nine to states, while North Caroline finished with the most wrestlers from a North Bayside school, qualifying six and two alternates.
"We had a rough Monday at Baysides," North Caroline head coach Robin Eaton said. "I preached to them all week 'That wasn't the week to shine. 'Work harder and fix a few things and we could shine at regionals.' And that's what they did. They did everything we worked on; wrestled very smart, wrestled tough. Didn't make mistakes."
North Caroline freshman Caleb Melvin (120), junior Corey Bunce (165) and senior Dakota Kinsey (285) each wrestled-back to win their respective consolation finals, while sophomores Darly Ortega (106), Connor Frank (113), and Jacob Carpenter (126) placed fourth.
Kent County senior Brady Sutton decisioned Harford Vo Tech's Nikolai Chervak in the 144-pound consolation final, and Cambridge-South Dorchester sophomore Mark Jones placed fourth at 285.

title: Fighting alive and well even if it's diminished
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Fighting alive and well even if it's diminished

 February 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1220
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Minnesota's Marcus Foligno took a hit, delivered one of his own to Chicago's Jarred Tinordi, and the two big guys dropped the gloves. Outdoors in front of 82,000 people in the Meadowlands, it took even less for Matt Rempe and Matt Martin to spice up the Rangers-Islanders showdown with a fight.When Morgan Rielly cross-checked Ridly Greig for firing a slap shot into an empty net? Some pushing and shoving. Nothing more.
"How there wasn't a brawl there, I don't know how everyone didn't start fighting," wondered Todd Simpson, a 50-year-old retired player who piled up more than 1,300 penalty minutes in 580 NHL games. "That should've been a big fight."
All of these situations were over the past month alone, riveting reminders that fighting is alive and well in the NHL even if it is diminished in many ways. It has been 20 years since Simpson and his Ottawa teammates got into a fight fest at Philadelphia, a game that still holds the NHL record with an astounding 419 penalty minutes. Of 40 players who suited up, 23 got at least two minutes of penalty time. Many got far more.
Those kinds of massive clashes are long gone, faded like the cheap shots and blood in "Slap Shot." Like the beloved movie, however, fighting is warmly remembered, even desired, by many fans of the game and cheering on the brawls remains common. Those fans need not worry: Even in the NHL, which has fewer and fewer spots for goons these days, fighting is rare but certainly not gone, with a fight coming roughly every four or five games across the league.
Many see a permanent place for it in a sport that values standing up for teammates, even as they have watched some of the biggest fighters left shells of themselves by repeated blows to the head.
"It doesn't happen often, but you still have to have it," said Vancouver Canucks coach Rick Tocchet, whose 237 career fights rank 21st all-time. "When I played, you could really use as intimidation. You can still use it a little bit today but not as much. The staged fighting and all that stuff, that doesn't work anymore. But there is a time and place for it."
FIGHTING ON THE WANEThe NHL does not publicly list penalties by type, including fighting and other major infractions. According to HockeyFights.com, there have been 219 fights this season through Monday with 63 more projected before the playoffs begin for a total of 282, which would be a sharp drop from the 789 in 2003-04. That is a 200% decrease over 20 years and significantly down from 645 as recently as 2010-11.
Rule changes are part of the reason. The institution of the salary cap in 2005 made it more difficult for a team to pay a player whose skills were limited to throwing punches and protecting stars. In 2013, it became illegal to take a helmet off to fight and mandatory visors were grandfathered in.
"It's obviously evolved a lot where guys like myself back in the day no longer exist — one-dimensional fighters no longer exist," said Riley Cote, who fought 50 times in 156 games with Philadelphia from 2007-10 and countless other times in the minor leagues. "It's been a natural progression. ... I'm not sure at the NHL level they'll ever fully phase it out, but they're doing a pretty good job of trying."
No one expects a fighting ban, like the ejection and suspension policies that exist in college and internationally. NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman has said the fighting helps keep tensions from boiling over.
"Fighting, in the spontaneous sense, tends to act as a bit of a thermostat when things happen in the course of the game," Bettman said in 2013. Discussing a fight between Jarome Iginla and Vincent Lecavalier, Bettman said, "I'd rather them be punching each other than swinging sticks at each other."
WILL FIGHTING SURVIVE?A 2011 survey by the NHL Players' Association and CBC found that 98% of players at that time didn't support the total elimination of fighting. A vast majority of those players are now out of the league, replaced by a generation that has made hockey faster and more skilled than ever — but still willing to drop the gloves on occasion and wanting that option.
"It always needs to be in the game," said St. Louis Blues captain Brayden Schenn, who has fought twice this season but never more than four times a year as a professional. "You need guys to police it themselves, and if you're going to run around and make a big hit, you've got to know that sometimes you're going to have to deal with the consequences."
That is certainly the opinion of Steve Oleksy, who HockeyFights.com credits with 107 bouts at various levels, including the NHL. He is 38 and retired and, after at least a couple of concussions and other wear and tear, is sometimes irritated in noisy places. Long drives and playing recreational sports is hard on his hands, which delivered hundreds of punches over the years.
He believes fighting will be virtually extinct a decade from now.
"I think it declines exponentially, but I also think the definition of a fight has changed so much," Oleksy said. "The number of actual punches, actual fights — what we would deem a fight back in the day — I just don't think that's there, either. And I think with that comes the rise in incidents like the cross-checking incident, slashing, two-handers, things like that."
Oleksy and many others point to junior hockey and even younger levels of hockey banning or at least discouraging and not teaching fighting as a bellwether for where things are going: Fewer players knowing how to, or being willing to, fight.
FIGHTING'S LEGACYLike many sports, hockey is facing the fallout from decades of its players suffering concussions and other traumatic brain injuries when safety wasn't the top priority it is now.
Patrick Sharp, who fought a handful of times as a player and is now in the Flyers' front office, said he cringes when he sees a player's helmet come off taking a heavy punch or banging their head on the ice. It's what happened to George Parros during a fight in 2013 that left him unconscious after falling face first.
The deaths of old-school enforcers like Derek Boogaard and Bob Probert, who were posthumously found to have chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE, has changed some minds when it comes to glorifying fighting the way it used to be. Oleksy contends that heavyweights of that vintage are no longer in the game and the risk of serious injury is much less now.
Dan Gallant, who has run HockeyFights.com since 2016, understands the business aspects of the decline of fighting and believes it to be cyclical. Now, general managers are looking for the next Milan Lucic or Tom Wilson — the big guy who can play hockey first but also can drop the gloves.
"The types of players that teams are going out and looking for to create that championship team have just kind of evolved," Gallant said, confident fighting will never totally disappear. "Who knows what tomorrow might bring, but I do believe that the players that played the game before, being in the game now and the players that are currently here will make sure that fighting does stay in some form or fashion."

title: Bucs' Tucker Claxton looks to 3rd straight title
author: LUKE BONANNI Special to the Bay Times Record Observer
content:
Bucs' Tucker Claxton looks to 3rd straight title

 February 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LUKE BONANNI Special to the Bay Times Record Observer | Section: News 
 
 445
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — Senior Tucker Claxton has committed to Mount Saint Mary's for the fall. Claxton was a key piece to the 2023 State Championship for Kent Island High School's varsity men's lacrosse team and also contributed to the 2022 team that took home the state prize. This spring Claxton looks to lead the Bucs to a third-straight title.Athletics at KIHS have been very competitive and successful over the last few years. After two amazing years for the Bucs with the 2022 and 2023 graduating classes, Claxton's commitment to the Class of 2024 is unparalleled.
Lacrosse might be Claxton's best sport, but he's also been on varsity football since sophomore year. In 2022, the Bucs were eliminated in the state quarterfinals and looked to bounce back in 2023. That's exactly what they did. Led by Kasey Heath and Claxton, alongside many other key players the Bucs had on their stacked roster, they were able to make the state championship before falling just short to Milford Mill Academy. Claxton stated, "There are a few memories that stick out to me. One was being a part of the first team in Kent Island football history to make the state championship. Another was running out of the tunnel to see a couple thousand people supporting you week in and week out. Breaking the receiving record for Kent Island school history was very cool as well." Claxton broke this record in his final high school game in a quarterfinal loss to Huntingtown. Claxton has also been a member of the varsity basketball team for the last two years.
When asked about playing three sports during his high school career, Claxton said, "I haven't had more than really a week off since Covid. I'm always doing something as soon as one season ends I was right on to another. Even the summer was filled with football camp, workouts, and club lacrosse. But this has taught me great discipline and mental toughness which I think is a hard lesson to find."
Last year, Claxton's role on the Buccaneer lacrosse team increased dramatically. His father, Andy Claxton, holds second place as the all-time leader in face off wins at the University of Maryland, and last season served as the offensive coordinator for Kent Island. The state championship in 2023 meant a lot to Tucker Claxton. "Scoring the game-winning goal in the state semifinals, and winning the state championship with my friends and teammates I've known since kindergarten meant a lot to me. From playing together the whole time, and being able to hug my dad after to celebrate, that was always the dream," he said.
Luke Bonanni is a student reporter from Kent Island High School.

title: PLACING THEMSELVES
author: Bill Haufe
content:
PLACING THEMSELVES

 February 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 773
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Last Monday's Bayside Conference championships was not one of the more memorable performances by Queen Anne's County High's young girls wrestling program."We didn't wrestle our best," Lions head coach John Waters said.
But Waters used Monday as a learning tool heading into Friday's Class 2A-1A East Regional championships.
"I think with a lot of young wrestlers, not knowing what Baysides mean, Monday was probably the best thing for us because it showed that the girls needed to be focused and ready for every match. A few of them at Baysides won their first match and they weren't ready for the semifinals."
The Lions certainly appeared ready Friday, placing in 11 of the 14 weight classes for a group that now advances to the Class 2A-1A state championships, beginning Thursday at the Show Place Arena in Upper Marlboro.
The top three finishers in each weight class in the four regional girls tournaments advance, where the boys tournaments advance the top four at each weight.
"Overall I'm proud of the girls," said Waters, who had 10 in the championship finals and left with four individual champs. "They really wrestled well. They've worked extremely hard to get where they are. Most of the girls on the team are first-year wrestlers. And if they're not first, they're second. So that says a lot about where they've come. Most of the varsity lineup are freshmen and sophomores."
Among that group, freshman Finley Patchett (125 pounds) and sophomore Bree Conard (115) each managed to win titles after being turned to their backs, as did junior Ally Conley (100).
"That just says a lot about their focus at practice this week," Waters said.
Conley (17-5) scored an early takedown against Parkside's Logan Newton (7-5), got turned, but recovered to earn a pin in 1 minute, 20 seconds to win the 100-pound crown. Conard (14-7) battled off her back and built a 10-4 lead before pinning Parkside's Brylee Davis (15-7) in 4:29 of the 115-pound final.
Then there was Patchett (13-4), who led 7-1 after one period against Stephen Decatur's Rachel Plata (9-2) in the 125-pound final. Patchett was leading 9-2 when Plata escaped, scored a takedown and picked up three near-fall points to close within 9-8 heading into the third. But Patchett, starting off bottom, hit a reversal 17 seconds into the third and added a late takedown for a 13-9 decision.
Junior Keira Corcoran (4-3) gave Queen Anne's a fourth champion when she pinned Decatur's Aya Mejber (2-11) in 3:45 to win the 135-pound championship. Corcoran got a takedown one minute into the match, but Mejber escaped to make it 2-1 entering the second period. Corcoran worked an escape 32 seconds into the second and got a takedown before earning her fall.
"We talked at practice about just being ready, staying focused," Waters said. "And doing what they're best at; not trying to do something they saw on Youtube or something. Just do what you're good at."
Queen Anne's got runner-up finishes from Ava Price (15-6) at 120, Delaney Gray (15-7) at 130, Julia Reburn (11-7) at 140, Lilly Hammond (14-5) at 145, Morgan Morris (5-6) at 170, and Kaylynn Bryant (17-4) at 190. Maggie Rooney (3-7) placed third at 235.
"There were a few matches, especially in the finals, we just came out a little flat," Waters said. "It's hard to come back unless you're ready. But the ones that lost in the finals, they'll have a couple good days of practice, they'll bounce back. They'll be ready. They'll refocus. That's what we're looking for."
Colonel Richardson will have the East's second largest contingent at states, as it qualified eight, led by junior Ryleigh Porter (9-3), who pinned Cambridge-South Dorchester's Sienna Mitchell (9-7) to win the 235-pound weight class.
Colonel's Dale Swann (17-8) lost by fall in the 105-pound final, but four teammates earned pins in the consolation finals.
Luna Infante-Reyes (11-13) pinned Kent County's Rhilynne Ashley-Pinder (4-11) in 4:44 of the 110-pound final. Frankie Aguiar (5-8) earned a 59-second fall over Decatur's Jessica Garcia (1-10) for third place at 120. Landine Dorleans (14-12) defeated James M. Bennett's Sinai Horsey (12-23) via a 2:35 pin at 125. And Olivia McGregor (17-2) wrestled back to earn a 3:46 fall over Queen Anne's Adelina Dickens (8-16) at 1:55.
Colonel's Annabelle Morales (2-11) and Danika Jeanty (4-9) won their consolation finals at 130 and 170, respectively with a bye.
Kent Island went two for two in the championship finals.
Sophomore Lilliana Mellinger (10-1) got a pair of takedowns before pinning Queen Anne's Price in 1:25 to win the 120-pound title. And senior Kendra Coffey (6-2) bundled two first-period takedowns with a second-period escape en route to a 5-2 decision over Queen Anne's Hammond in the 145-pound final.

title: Sabres rally, reach conference final
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Sabres rally, reach conference final

 February 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 587
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Saints Peter and Paul High boys head basketball coach Gary Gould praised Robbie Cunningham for stepping up Thursday night.Perhaps the biggest of those steps came with less than 90 seconds remaining in a two-point ballgame, when Cunningham dove to make a steal that Garett Hemingway converted into a layup to help give the Sabres breathing room in an eventual 56-49 victory over Cristo Rey in a Maryland Interscholastic Athletic Association C Conference semifinal.
Sts. Peter & Paul (15-8) advances to Saturday's MIAA C Conference championship, where it will meet the winner between Beth Tfiloh and Park at 8 p.m. at the University of Maryland Baltimore County's Chesapeake Employers Insurance Arena in Baltimore.
"Robbie Cunningham. Wow," Gould said. "He stepped up tonight. Defensively, he must have had five or six steals. He's that guy for us. He's that three-tool guy. Awesome."
Cunningham, who finished with a game-high 23 points, scored off a Brayden Smith assist with 3:42 remaining to give the Sabres a 49-44 lead.
Cristo Rey's Cobi Woolson (15 points) scored on consecutive drives to pull the Hornets (10-10) within 49-48 with 1:45 left.
Hemingway (17 points) scored on a drive to make it 51-48, but was called for a technical foul for taunting. Woolson made one of two free throws, keeping it a one-possession game with 1:28 left. Cristo Rey got the ball off the technical, but as it tried working the ball on the left side, Cunningham dove and knocked the ball away. Hemingway grabbed it, raced down the floor and scored a layup for a 53-49 lead with 1:01 left.
"I've been nervous all day because this could end our season," Cunningham said. "And we just had to go out there and get it for the seniors. We came out on top. Defense wins games. We've just been working on defense. Usually it's just one person playing defense. Tonight everybody played defense."
The Hornets threw an errant pass on their next possession and quickly fouled Cunningham on the inbounds. Cunningham hit both free throws with 16.7 seconds left to make it 55-49 Sabres, then added one more free throw with two seconds left.
"Today was a weird day all day," Gould said. "I was nervous the whole time, understanding what could happen. I didn't understand what we were going to do because this type of game brings extra pressure."
Behind Grant Wheeler (team-high 18 points), the Hornets built a 16-9 lead in the first quarter, and took a 23-21 lead into the locker room.
A pull-up jumper and a 3-pointer from Wheeler extended Cristo Rey's lead to 33-28 with 2:41 remaining in the third quarter. But Sts. Peter & Paul outscored the Hornets, 9-4, over the remainder of the period to knot the game at 37-all heading into the fourth quarter.
Smith (nine points) connected for a 3-pointer to nudge the Sabres to a 40-37 lead. Wheeler responded with a trey to tie the game. Cunningham then swished a 3, pushing Sts. Peter & Paul back in front. A free throw from Machi Grahm and two from Wheeler tied the game again at 43-43.
But free throws from Cunningham and K'den Spears pushed Sts. Peter & Paul to a 45-44 lead it never surrendered over the final five minutes.
"We're a team that builds throughout the game, and eventually wear you down," said Gould, whose team outscored the Hornets, 19-12 in the fourth quarter. "And I think in the fourth quarter we finally got to that part where we found their weakness. And when we went to the box-in-on it slowed them down too."

title: BACK ON TOP
author: Bill Haufe
content:
BACK ON TOP

 February 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1013
 Words 

 Read News Document

 SALISBURY —Many in the crowd that jammed into the Wicomico Youth & Civic Center for Tuesday night's Bayside Conference boys basketball championship between Stephen Decatur and Cambridge-South Dorchester High figured the game was a mere formality in the Seahawks' coronation as kings of the hardwood.Uh, the Vikings were not part of that crowd.
"They had Decatur beating us by 25," Cambridge-SD junior forward Koby Ennals said of Bayside forecasters.
"We were 25-point underdogs," Vikings head coach Shawn Tucker said. "But that's why you play."
Crashing the boards like every rebound carried a prize, Cambridge-SD played with a fever-like intensity from baseline to baseline en route a 70-57 victory that gave the Vikings their first outright conference title since 1996.
"We just didn't match their intensity," Decatur head coach B.J. Johnson said of the Vikings. "Congratulations to Coach Tucker and Cambridge. They just wanted it more than we did in my honest opinion."
Though Cambridge-SD shared the 2003 conference crown with Pocomoke, it had lost in its last seven trips to the Bayside final.
Many figured that string would be extended as the Class 3A Seahawks came in riding an 11-game win streak.
"Nobody in this gym but a couple of people believed that we were going to win this game. And they were probably all from up North," Tucker said after the Vikings improved to 20-1.
Cambridge-SD's fan base may have had its faith shaken early as Decatur (19-2) opened an 8-0 lead less than four minutes into the game, and carried a 16-10 lead into the second quarter.
Led by guard Anthony Hughes, Cambridge-SD started hitting the boards harder and attacking the offensive rim more in the second quarter.
"Anthony Hughes played his butt off," Tucker said. "For a 6-(foot)-1 guard, he rebounded like he was 6-foot-7. This kid just gave us everything. And that's what we've been preaching."
Baskets by Ennals (game-high 21 points) and senior guard LaShaun Moody (18 points), and two free throws from Sterling Perkins (12) pulled the Vikings even at 16-all less than two minutes into the second quarter.
Davin Chandler (15 points) put the Seahawks back in front. But Hughes (nine points) scored on a double-pump shot to tie the game, then watched Moody make a three-point play for the Vikings' first lead at 21-18.
A three-point play from Brycen Coleman (team-high 18 points) drew Decatur even at 21-21. The mercurial Moody put Cambridge-SD back in front at 23-21. But Chandler and Brogan Eastlack hit back-to-back 3-pointers for the Seahawks. Chandler then scored on a drive that stoked Decatur's fans and moved the South Bayside champs to a 29-23 lead with 1:24 left in the first half.
The Vikings seemed unfazed. Perkins hit a 3-pointer, was fouled, and hit the free throw to complete a four-point play with 46.5 seconds left. Cambridge-SD then got what Tucker considered a game-changing 3-pointer from Thomas Wilson with 19 seconds left, giving the Vikings a 30-29 halftime lead.
"The 3-pointer that Thomas Wilson hit in the first half. We went up 30-29 and I saw Decatur's body language, like 'Another guy we've got to account for?'" Tucker said. "That's when I knew."
Hughes also had a feeling.
"We held them to 29 points at the half," Hughes said. "Coach told us if we keep them at 29 like that we're going to win the game. And that's what happened."
Trybe Wise's free throw seven seconds into the second half forged the game's fourth and final tie at 30-all. Twenty-five seconds later, Darren Belizare scored inside, giving Cambridge-SD a lead it never relinquished the rest of the game. Ennals followed with a layup. Hughes scored inside for a 36-30 Cambridge-SD lead.
Decatur called time and got a layup from Coleman out of the break. But Perkins splashed a 3-pointer and Hughes muscled inside for a score and a 41-32 lead that prompted another Decatur timeout.
"We came in with a great mindset tonight, thinking that we were going to win," Hughes said. "We knew we had to crash (the boards) and get the rebounds tonight because they were taller. We had to box out, play together, play relentless."
Cambridge-SD continued to do all three.
A 7-2 run got Decatur within four at 43-39 with under two minutes to go in the third. But the Vikings answered the last basket of that run, and the Seahawks' other two field goals of the period, to take a 49-43 lead into the fourth.
"Coming into this game everybody said their size was going to be the problem, but in all actuality it wasn't," said Moody, who buried a 3-pointer 1:24 into the final period for a 52-43 Cambridge-SD lead. "We were equally matched up. We boxed out hard. Anthony Hughes got us great rebounds in the stretch. I think that's where we won this game with the rebounds. It didn't come from offense. It came from defense and getting our rebounds.
The Vikings continued to use that combination to their advantage over the final six minutes, forcing turnovers, pounding the glass on both ends, and often limiting the Seahawks to just one shot a possession.
"That's our calling card," Tucker said of his defense. "We just turn people over. Sometimes our offense can get a little stagnant, but we turn people over. That's our offense."
Decatur closed within 55-50 on a Chandler bucket with 3:47 left. Ennals' 3-pointer and a basket by Belizare pushed Cambridge-SD's lead back to 10 at 60-50 with just over three minutes left. Back-to-back baskets by Careen Bolden (10 points) again narrowed the Viking lead to six. But Ennals scored off a Perkins miss and Moody hit two free throws to make it 64-54.
Wise hit a jumper to get the Seahawks within 64-57 with 1:13 left, but the Vikings cemented the win, hitting six of eight free-throw attempts over the final 1:10.
"We've been preaching the last couple of days, and it's been in our scouting report: match their physicality," Tucker said. "And that's what we did tonight. We matched their physicality. Those guys, they're resilient. We had a couple of guys go down that play a lot of minutes, but they still found a way to win this game. I just love those guys' resiliency."

title: Late surge lifts Wi-Hi past Lions
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Late surge lifts Wi-Hi past Lions

 February 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 652
 Words 

 Read News Document

 SALISBURY — It had been 12 days since its undefeated season was stopped cold via a 40-point shellacking from unbeaten Wicomico.Now, just 11 seconds into the fourth quarter of a seesaw Bayside Conference championship, Queen Anne's County High's girls basketball team was holding a one-point lead over that same Wi-Hi bunch Tuesday night. But the Lions' hopes for a second conference crown in three years virtually evaporated over the next four minutes, as the Indians went on a 13-0 run that proved fuel enough for a 58-52 victory at the Wicomico Youth & Civic Center.
"It was a great game," Queen Anne's head coach Mike Kern said after Wicomico had earned its first conference championship since 1985.
Routed 81-41 by Wi-Hi on Feb. 8, Queen Anne's (19-2) took a quick 5-0 lead Tuesday, prompting Indians head coach Willie Downing to burn a timeout with only 28 seconds elapsed. The Lions never trailed in the first half, and carried a 25-23 lead into halftime.
The game became a back-and-forth contest in the third period, with five lead changes and two ties. A pair of Taylor Jordan free throws pulled Queen Anne's even at 36-36 with 1:08 remaining in the third. But Wicomico sophomore guard Se'Lah Foreman (game-high 26 points) hit a 3-pointer just 12 seconds later for a 39-36 Indians lead.
A transition layup from freshman guard Kariana Hickson (team-high 20 points) with 12 seconds left in the third quarter, and freshman Laila Coles' drive 11 seconds into the fourth nudged Queen Anne's to a 40-39 lead.
But Foreman and Wi-Hi (21-0) took over from there.
In one of the few defensive lapses of the game, Foreman was left alone and canned a 3-pointer with 7:37 left in the game for a 42-40 Wicomico lead. A Lions turnover led to Carlisa Johnson scoring inside. Foreman converted a steal into a layup. Gabrielle Corbin (10 points) then scored on a put-back, giving the Indians a 48-40 lead, drawing a Queen Anne's timeout.
Wi-Hi wasn't quite through.
Another Lions turnover led to an inside bucket from Sariah Sanon. Foreman then got behind the Queen Anne's defense for an easy breakaway layup and a 52-40 lead with a little over four minutes to play.
"What really hurt us is the fourth quarter, leaving Foreman open for that wide-open three, and then she got a couple breakaways," Kern said. "We weren't marked up well and had some mental lapses there, and they got some easy baskets out of it. That turned a one-point (Queen Anne's) lead into a (12)-point (Wi-Hi) lead and it was hard to fight back."
Jordan's basket with 3:44 left ended a four-plus minute Lions' scoring drought, but the Indians answered with baskets from Jecolia Traore (eight points) and Johnson (eight points) for a 56-42 cushion with under three minutes remaining.
"The big thing we talked about at halftime was stop hesitating, because it was like they were overthinking what we were doing," Downing said. "Once they did that part and just started relaxing, the defense picked it up. Once they got active on defense, they didn't have time to think about anything else."
Queen Anne's consistently drove to the basket, but often had shots rejected by Sanon or Corbin, who together accounted for the bulk of Wi-Hi's 15 blocked shots.
"We were hoping to get them in foul trouble and we ended up in foul trouble," said Kern, who watched Coles draw her fourth foul early in the third quarter and RJ Ensor foul out midway through the fourth. "That hurt us a little bit."
The Lions were also hurt at the free-throw line, where they converted 14 of 25 attempts.
"Foul shooting we struggled," Kern said. "If we had shot better it would have been a different score."
Queen Anne's did manage to outscore the Indians, 10-2, over the final 2:48, with freshman Bea Holthaus hitting a free throwing to put the finishing touches on a 15-point, 10-rebound performance.
"I was proud we did fight back," Kern said.

title: Playoff push arrives as season hits final stretch
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Playoff push arrives as season hits final stretch

 February 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 920
 Words 

 Read News Document

 There's no NBA player who is a bigger fan of harness racing than Denver's Nikola Jokic. He owns horses, goes to tracks whenever he can and even accepted one of his MVP awards while riding around at his farm in Serbia.He knows the stretch run often decides races.
And the same holds true in the NBA, which is entering its stretch run.
The All-Star break is over, games resume on Thursday and the defending champion Nuggets — along with a slew of other contenders — are hoping that this is the time when they can start hitting their best stride. Denver is coming out of the break in fourth place in the Western Conference, three games back of No. 1 Minnesota.
"We don't try to listen to what people say," Jokic said. "We know what we are capable of. And it's working for us. So, I don't know what people are saying, that we are not good. I don't say that we are the best, but we are not bad."
They were the best last season. This season, the best won't be crowned until June, of course. The next couple of months are all about jostling for playoff position — or in some cases, fighting for playoff spots.
It's not the second half — what people commonly call the period after the All-Star break — but rather the final third of the season. The league is exactly two-thirds of the way through the season, 820 games down, 410 games to go. It's the time of year when playbooks tend to get tweaked a little and things get a little more serious.
Paul George of the Los Angeles Clippers knows the playoff push is underway. But as a veteran, he also knows that the most important game is always the next one.
"Can't look too far ahead," George said. "Take it one game at a time. Because that's what you tend to do, second half of the season, start to look ahead and look forward to playoffs and just trying to get to the playoffs. But we just got to take it one game at a time."
Boston has the NBA's best record and sits high atop the Eastern Conference, Minnesota and Oklahoma City — a pair of surprises — are first and second, respectively, in the West and some teams with championship pedigrees like Golden State and the Los Angeles Lakers are hoping their pre-All-Star momentum carries over now.
The Warriors were 8-2 in their last 10 games before the break, the Lakers 7-3.
"The most important thing for me is definitely my health, where I'm at right now, where our team is leaning," Lakers forward LeBron James said. "We're trending in the right direction. Obviously, with our Laker team, it's been about health all year. Trying to do what's best for me for the betterment of the team."
He's been dealing with an ankle issue that limited him in the All-Star Game but didn't prevent him from playing. Other teams have far bigger concerns — primarily the Philadelphia 76ers, who spent a bit of time in November atop the East but have dropped nine of their last 12 games with reigning MVP Joel Embiid out with a knee injury.
They're sliding and so are the Milwaukee Bucks, who have gone 3-7 since Doc Rivers took over as coach. Rivers said at All-Star weekend that he knew that taking over a team just before a long road trip would be a mistake; it seems like he was right. But he also believes there's time to figure things out.
"If you look statistically over the last 20 years, the same teams win it: the teams that are in the top five or 10 in offense and the teams that are in the top five or 10 in defense," Rivers said. "That's not going away. So you can score all you want. But you better be able to defend, too, if you want to win."
Boston has a six-game lead over second-place Cleveland in the East; that would suggest it's safe to go ahead and put the Celtics down for a 10th consecutive playoff berth, extending the longest current streak of postseason appearances in the league.
Detroit, Washington, Charlotte, San Antonio, Portland and Memphis all are alive mathematically but not realistically. Take them out of the mix, and it's 24 teams left in the race for 20 spots when including the play-in tournament.
The Thunder had 100-1 odds to win the NBA title when the season started. They're at 25-1 now, according to FanDuel Sportsbook.
"I think we're starting to kind of see others take notice of us," Thunder guard and MVP candidate Shai Gilgeous-Alexander said. "We knew that was going to happen once we started winning games. It comes with the territory."
Every team has between 26 and 29 games left to play. In terms of combined remaining opponent winning percentage, Orlando, Miami and Boston are among the teams with the easiest — on paper, anyway — schedules the rest of the way. Phoenix would have the toughest, including two games left to play against Boston and a 10-game stretch to end the season all against likely playoff teams.
"We respect every team regardless and try to focus on us as much as possible each night," Suns forward Kevin Durant said. "It just about building our habits, getting better at what we've already established and pushing forward. I think playing against some of the teams that's going to be there at the end of the season, it's going to be a great test before we head to the playoffs."

title: Cougars look to extend Top 25 stay, face Arizona
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Cougars look to extend Top 25 stay, face Arizona

 February 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: News 
 
 786
 Words 

 Read News Document

 No. 21 Washington State, back in the Top 25 for first time in 16 years, eyes trip to No. 4 ArizonaWashington State coach Kyle Smith had just finished watching his team almost entirely shut down Stanford last weekend, and win for the 10th time in its last 11 games, when he made a rare admission for college basketball coaches.
"Right now," Smith said, "this is the best team we've had in five years."
The No. 21 Cougars can underscore just how good they are Thursday night, when they carry their first AP Top 25 ranking since the 2007-08 season into a Pac-12 showdown with fourth-ranked Arizona. Washington State sprung an upset in Tucson last year, when the Wildcats also were in the top five, and beat the perennial heavyweight in January in Pullman, Washington.
"We've done it before, but it's the hardest place to play in the country," said Smith, who took the Cougars to back-to-back NITs but has his sights set firmly on their first NCAA Tournament bid since that 2008 team lost to North Carolina in the Sweet 16.
"It's going to be loud and crazy, and that's probably the No. 1 challenge: Can we handle that?" Smith said. "They're good at home, and they're fast and they're athletic. And they're big. Did I mention that? We'll give it a good go, see what happens."
Only good things have been happening lately for long-suffering Washington State (20-6, 11-3), which sits a half-game back of the Wildcats (20-5, 11-3) as the Pac-12 schedule hits the homestretch. The Cougars' only loss since the first week of January came in overtime at California, and they avenged that loss in a rout last week.
The last time they had a 10-1 stretch in conference play was during the 1940-41 season, when they had a 13-1 streak in the old Pacific Coast Conference. That team lost to Wisconsin 39-34 in the national championship game.
"We appreciate it," Cougars forward Andrej Jakimovski said, "but I think we're just taking it day by day and game by game.
"Obviously we have a lot of compliments," Jakimovski added, "and there are people asking, like, 'What's the difference from this team and last year's, or the year before?' And I'm always saying: 'We have such a good group of guys. We love each other, on and off the court.' You can see the connection we have, and that's the beauty of this team."
The difference is bearing out in win-loss column. The Cougars need two wins to match the team two years ago that won 22 but needed a run to the NIT semifinals to get there, and three would give them their most wins since going 26-9 in 2008.
So while many coaches might demure when they are asked to compare teams, Smith hardly seemed to have a problem calling this year's bunch "the best team we've had in five years." Because the truth is, there really is no comparison.
BRUTAL BIG 12
Iowa State moved up to No. 6 in the AP Top 25 on Monday, the highest ranking for the Cyclones since Dec. 14, 2015, and just in time to face second-ranked Houston in yet another massive showdown in the brutal Big 12.
The Cyclones at least get a reprieve — if there is such a thing — when they play last-place West Virginia this weekend. Houston follows with a trip to No. 11 Baylor for the only scheduled meeting between those schools this season.
Speaking of the Bears, they have to visit No. 25 BYU on Tuesday night.
SEC ON THE RISE
The Big 12 is starting to feel some pressure from the Southeastern Conference when it comes to conference superiority. The football heavyweight has six teams in the AP Top 25 after Florida entered the poll at No. 24 this week, matching the Big 12 for the most of any league.
The Gators will take their ranking on the road Wednesday when they play No. 13 Alabama, which began the week with one-game lead over Tennessee in the SEC race. Florida has won three straight while the Crimson Tide have won six of their last seven.
Alabama's tough week continues on Saturday, when it plays No. 17 Kentucky at Rupp Arena.
WINNING STREAKS TO WATCH
UConn was voted the unanimous No. 1 in the AP Top 25 on Monday, thanks in part to its nation-leading 14-game winning streak. The Huskies will try to keep it alive through a trip to No. 15 Creighton on Tuesday night and a visit from Villanova on Saturday.
No. 18 Saint Mary's has a tough week ahead as it tries to extend a 13-game winning streak. The Gales play San Francisco, which is 20-6 and two games back of them in the West Coast standings, on Tuesday before playing San Diego on Saturday.

title: HOME RULE

content:
HOME RULE

 February 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Home Rule

 BERLIN — Now that a fifth consecutive state dual-meet championship has been tucked away, Stephen Decatur High head wrestling coach Josh August said his team can focus on individual competition at the regional and state levels, though the approach is slightly different."There are certain things that you would do," August said, comparing dual-meet to individual competition. "If you're losing, you don't give up the bonus, or you don't get pinned in a dual meet because that score matters. But out here, like if you're down, sometimes you got to let it fly. You might not get the takedown but you went for it. The mentality is a little different, but overall just go out, wrestle tough, get to the positions you prefer. Most of the time things work out pretty good for you."
Things again worked out pretty good for the Seahawks Monday, as they placed nine in the finals and left with seven individual titles on the way to winning their fifth straight Bayside Conference championship in their home gym.
Decatur totaled 269½ points to easily outdistance runner-up Parkside by 86½ points. Kent Island was third with 179½ points, followed by North Caroline (fourth, 166), Colonel Richardson (fifth, 146½) and Queen Anne's County (sixth, 123).
"They are just a really tight team," August said. "The momentum from state duals definitely kind of bleeds over into this."
Decatur reached the finals in the first five weight classes, with Juan Hinojosa (33-3) leading off with a fall over Kent Island freshman Gavin Lindner (27-10) in 1 minute, 47 seconds in the 106-pound title match. Elijah Collick (35-2) followed with a 16-4 major decision over Queen Anne's freshman Alan McDonald (30-7) in the 113 final. Liam Hugues (14-5) made it three straight titles for the Seahawks with a 7-1 decision over Wicomico's Tavenon Outlaw (29-7) at 120.
Decatur's Reid Caimi (32-2) advanced to the 126-pound final but forfeited to Queen Anne's senior Tremaine Jackson (32-3) due to injury.
The Seahawks' win streak ended at 132, where Kent Island's Greg Couch (27-7) scored takedowns in each period for a 7-0 victory over Decatur's Aaron August (29-5).
"He's been wrestling 38 for most of this year," Kent Island head coach Tommy Sitar said of Couch. "He came down and had a great day."
Amarian Manuel (34-8) gave Decatur its fourth individual crown with a 9-2 decision over Parkside's Xavier Moorman (19-3) at 150. Teammate Gavin Solito (39-1) built a 7-1 lead before pinning Kent Island's Brandon Adler (22-12) in the 157-pound final. Senior Parker Intrieri (28-2) completed the Seahawks' second three-match win streak of the finals, earning a 14-1 major decision over Colonel Richardson sophomore Derrick Mitchell (32-7) at 165.
Two bouts later, Decatur senior Kole Kohut (32-6) pieced together a 12-4 major decision over Kent Island's Nick Morey (32-5) to win the 190-pound weight class.
The only other teams with multiple winners were Kent Island and Parkside.
The Bucs got their second crown from senior Giuseppe Mellinger (33-5), who after surrendering an escape to Parkside's Canaan Mapp (22-7), strung together a second-period takedown, with an escape and another takedown in the third period en route to a 7-2 decision at 175.
"Giuseppe, another awesome tournament," said Sitar, who had six in the finals, including Cody Sandefer (29-9), the runner-up at 144. "We were kind of hoping we'd get seven in there today, but I'm pretty happy with the effort. Those guys that didn't make it for the most part wrestled back pretty well. I'm proud of our team score."
Parkside got pinfalls from Shaheed Armstrong (33-6) and Ali'i Turner (24-5) to win the 215- and 285-pound titles, respectively, and nudge past Kent Island for second place in the team standings.
Kent County sophomore Scottie Ford (34-1) was the fourth wrestler from a North Bayside school to win a title, as he crafted a 6-0 decision over Parkside's Rocco Tully (33-8) to win the 138-pound weight class.
North Caroline's fourth-place finish was bolstered by eight top-four finishes, including four winners in the consolation finals — Darly Ortega (106), Edward Darling (157), Tommy Morris (215) and Daketa Kinsey (285).
Sophomore Chatydrick Pickrom (23-13) gave Colonel Richardson a second finalist in the boys' competition as he reached the 285-pound final, where he lost to Turner.
"I would say it's definitely up there," Colonel Richardson head coach Bryan Hall said of the Colonel's fifth-place finish possibly being its best in conference tournament history for his program. "They did very well. We only had one guy that didn't place in the top seven."
The Colonels also finished with four champions in the girls division. Dale Swann (16-7) pinned Decatur's Melanie Ruiz (5-8) in 1:16 to win the 105-pound crown. Freshman Olivia McGregor (15-1) pinned Queen Anne's Lilly Hammond (14-5) in 3:26 to win the 145-pound division. Teammate Hannah Kefauver (9-7) almost duplicated that effort, pinning Decatur's Amari Purnell (9-4) in 3:25 of the 155-pound final.
"They wrestled well," Hall said of his girls. "We kind of expected Olivia McGregor to win. She only lost one match on the season. The finals match she wrestled very tough. She was down early and was able to come back and pin the girl.
"Hannah, she really showed up," Hall continued. "She showed a lot of grit, wrestled hard, beat two tough girls. And Dale of course, I think she beat everyone in the weight class, so she beat them all again."
Ryleigh Porter (7-3) was Colonel's fourth champ, but the only other wrestler in the 235-pound weight class dropped out of the tournament. Colonel's Luna Infante-Reyes (110), Landine Dorleans (125) and Danika Jeanty (170) each placed second.
Lilliana Mellinger (8-1) gave Kent Island its lone girls champion when she earned a 10-5 victory over Queen Anne's Ava Price (15-6) in the 120-pound final.
Queen Anne's finished with three conference champions, including Ally Conley (17-5) — the 2022 2A-1A state champion — who pinned Parkside's Logan Newton (7-4) in 30 seconds to win the 100-pound title.
The Lions' other two finals wins came against teammates. Keira Corcoran (4-3) earned a 3-2 decision over Linda Vail (7-9) to win the 135-pound weight class, and Julia Reburn (12-6) pinned Emma Coppage (2-8) in the 140-pound final.
"Overall I would say it was a great day for girls wrestling in the Bayside, finally getting the tournament going," said Queen Anne's boys head coach David Stricker, who has played a key role in the growth of girls wrestling in the state. "Team-wise we did pretty well. I think we kind of underachieved a little bit. We had a rough semifinals and finals. It was sort of a reality check for some of our girls going into regionals Friday."

title: POWER SURGE
author: Bill Haufe
content:
POWER SURGE

 February 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 748
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WYE MILLS — With less than six minutes off the clock Friday night, Chesapeake College men's head basketball coach Andrew Sachs called time to deliver a blunt, two-word message to his team with the volume on high."It's February," Sachs roared at the group seated in front of him.
The Skipjacks apparently caught their coach's drift, going on a 30-13 first-half run, then piecing together a staggering 21-1 second-half blitz that fueled a 78-63 victory over Potomac State (West Virginia) College.
"You got to be playing your best basketball at the end of the season," said Sachs after Chesapeake improved to 13-14 overall, 7-3 in Region 20.
That's not how this one started though for the Skipjacks, as the Catamounts (8-13, 4-6) connected on three 3-pointers in the opening six minutes to build a 13-6 lead.
"They're the second best three-point shooting team in the league," Sachs said of Potomac State. "That's what they do well. And they were spreading us out too much, so I had to get up and get some ball pressure. We haven't played a lot of man recently; trying to keep my big guys out of foul trouble."
Two nights after dropping 13 3-pointers on Cecil, Chesapeake began finding its range from behind the arc, hitting six treys during a 30-13 surge that turned a 13-6 deficit into a 36-26 lead with 4:30 play in the first half.
Marquis McAbee scored on a drive before freshman Armani Martin (game-high 28 points) splashed back-to-back 3-pointers to give Chesapeake a lead it never surrendered at 16-15. Skipjack sophomore center Azim Sana (nine points, 20 rebounds) scored inside then watched Martin bury the third of his five 3-pointers for a 19-15 lead.
"It's kind of our trademark," Sachs said of the 3-pointer.
Andre Stewart's trey with 7:26 left in the first half moved the Skipjacks to a 24-17 lead. A pair of 3-pointers from Rodney Vilsaint (team-high 15 points) — the second of which was part of a four-point play — kept Potomac State close at 26-24 with 6:21 remaining in the first half. But Stewart and Martin each stuck 3-pointers during a 10-2 surge that pushed Chesapeake's lead to 36-26 with 4:30 to play.
Chesapeake carried a 10-point lead into halftime, leading 42-32.
Potomac State rallied, pulling within 50-48, when Camren Wilkes (12 points) hit a jumper with 11:06 remaining. But the Catamounts went the next 5:20 without a basket from the floor, as Chesapeake took command with a 21-1 scoring spree, which featured four more 3-pointers, including two from Josh Rivers (17 points) and another from Martin that rolled around the rim before falling. Martin capped the run with a pretty baseline spin and drive to the bucket for a 71-49 cushion.
"It helps when you get stops," Sachs said of the 21-1 run. "And then we had two threes that went in that bounced around every inch of the rim. So that helped too. That's home cooking right there.
"But we do a lot of shooting," Sachs continued. "For guys to play at the next level they got to be able to shoot the basketball. If you can't shoot you're really limited offensively on how you can help a team, unless I'm going to be able to clear sides for you and you get to the foul line. But our free-throw shooting has been really poor this year. It's really hurt us."
Though not spectacular, Chesapeake was 10 of 16 from the foul line for the game. But a facet Sachs was real pleased with was the Skipjacks ability to value the basketball.
"We only had nine turnovers tonight, which is good for us because we've averaged 17," Sachs said. "That's been part of our issue all year long is we turn the ball over a lot; we don't make free throws. It's hard to win games like that."
Another stat Sachs may have found satisfying was that after watching Potomac State connect on five first-half 3-pointers, the Catamounts managed just two in the second half.
Currently behind Howard, Catonsville and Southern of Maryland in league play, Chesapeake could potentially clinch a home regional playoff game with a home win Wednesday against Northern Virginia.
"We just got to keep getting better," said Sachs, who after Northern Virginia on Wednesday hosts Howard on Friday before playing at Garrett on Sunday. "You win two out of three you're playing at home. You win one more you're at least going to be in the tournament. And you win all three you'll finish in second or third, or maybe even first. You never know."

title: Terps coaching great Driesell dies
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Terps coaching great Driesell dies

 February 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1514
 Words 

 Read News Document

 COLLEGE PARK — Lefty Driesell, the Hall of Fame coach whose folksy drawl belied a fiery on-court demeanor that put Maryland on the college basketball map and enabled him to rebuild several struggling programs, died Saturday. He was 92.Driesell died at his home in Virginia Beach, Virginia, his family said.
Maryland honored Driesell with a moment of silence before its game against No. 14 Illinois Saturday. The team wore throwback uniforms from the 1970s previously worn on Jan. 21, when the Terrapins honored Driesell with an "Ode to Lefty."
Driesell finished with 786 victories over parts of five decades and was the first coach to win more than 100 games at four NCAA Division I schools. He started at Davidson in 1960 before bringing Maryland into national prominence from 1969-86, a stay that ended with the cocaine-induced death of All-American Len Bias.
Driesell then won five regular-season conference titles over nine seasons at James Madison and finished with a successful run at Georgia State from 1997 to 2003.
"His contributions to the game go way beyond wins and losses, and he won a lot," former Duke coach Mike Krzyzewski said after Driesell finally made the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2018. "It's an honor he's deserved for a long time."
Driesell launched the college basketball tradition known as Midnight Madness on Oct. 15, 1971. At three minutes after midnight on the first day of practice as sanctioned by the NCAA, Driesell had his players take a mandatory mile run on the track inside the Maryland football stadium.
The lighting was provided by the headlights of a few cars parked at one end of the stadium. The motivation came from Driesell's prodding and the estimated 800 students who gathered to watch the unpublicized event.
"I've done a lot of crazy things to get attention, but that wasn't one of them," Driesell said years later. "I was just trying to get an early jump on practice. I had no idea what it was going to lead to."
Driesell also helped knock down racial barriers in the college game. He made George Raveling the first Black coach in the Atlantic Coast Conference by hiring him as an assistant in 1969. Driesell's effort to recruit Charlie Scott to play at Davidson helped make the future NBA star become the first African American scholarship athlete to attend North Carolina.
Scott initially committed to Davidson before choosing UNC but acknowledged that Driesell paved the way.
"I think if there had never been a Lefty Driesell, there would never have been a Charlie Scott attending North Carolina," said Scott, who joined the Hall of Fame in 2018 with Driesell. "My commitment to go to Davidson really opened up all the other schools in the recruiting process."
Race played no factor in Driesell's effort to recruit the best players.
"He did so many great things in marketing the game and opened up so many doors for many African Americans players and coaches like myself," said Len Elmore, who played for Driesell at Maryland from 1971-74. "Lefty was a trailblazer and an innovator."
Walking onto the court at Maryland to the tune of "Hail to the Chief," Driesell would thrust both arms in the air — two fingers extended on each hand with the V for victory sign — amid a standing ovation. On the sideline, he would often stomp his foot to show his displeasure with a call, and if things got really intense he would peel off his sports jacket, toss it to the floor and trample it.
Yet, Driesell rarely raised his voice off the court and had a knack for charming the parents of potential recruits with an assuring, homespun style that smacked of his Southern roots.
"He had a big personality, was an excellent recruiter and he helped put Maryland basketball on the map," said Brad Davis, a guard at Maryland from 1974-77 before heading to the NBA.
Driesell was inducted into the College Basketball Hall of Fame in 2007, but his entry into the Naismith shrine proved more elusive. He was a finalist four times before receiving the necessary 75% vote three months after his 86th birthday. The long snub, many speculated, came because Driesell was forced to resign at Maryland in 1986 after Bias overdosed on cocaine in a campus dorm after being drafted by the Boston Celtics.
Maryland had to pay Driesell for the rest of his 10-year contract because it could find no wrongdoing on his part. But his departure meant Driesell never got to fulfill the declaration he made upon taking over in College Park — he would make Maryland the "UCLA of the East."
Under Driesell, the Terrapins didn't enjoy the success John Wooden had at UCLA. Maryland failed to reach the Final Four during his 17-year stay, but the Terps won or shared five ACC regular-season titles and captured the league tournament in 1984 — on Driesell's fifth trip to the final.
Looking back on his "UCLA of the East" boast, Driesell quipped: "I was kind of drunk or something when I said it. But we were pretty good and we wound up pretty good. We had a lot of great players."
Before Driesell arrived at Maryland, the team was an ACC doormat and had trouble drawing fans to old Cole Field House. After going 13-13 in Driesell's first season, the Terps announced their resurgence on Jan. 9, 1971, with a 31-30 overtime upset of No. 2 South Carolina at home. There was no shot clock then, so Driesell ordered his players to slow the game to a crawl against a team that had defeated Maryland 96-70 just three weeks earlier.
One of Driesell's best teams never made it to the postseason. In the 1974 ACC championship game, the fourth-ranked Terrapins lost in overtime to No. 1 North Carolina State 103-100 during a time when only the conference champion advanced to the NCAA Tournament.
A week later, a Maryland team featuring future NBA starters Tom McMillen, John Lucas and Elmore turned down a bid to the NIT, which it had won two years earlier. N.C. State went on to win the 1974 NCAA title, ending UCLA's seven-year streak as national champions.
"Lefty's team that year," Krzyzewski said, "was probably as good as 20 national champions."
Born on Christmas Day in 1931, Charles Grice Driesell grew up in Norfolk, Virginia. He was a star basketball player for Granby High in Norfolk before attending Duke.
After working at the Ford Motor Co., Driesell took a job as a junior varsity football and basketball coach at Granby in 1954 after convincing his wife, Joyce, that he could withstand the pay cut by also selling encyclopedias. He eventually was promoted to head coach of the varsity team before moving to Newport News High, where he won 57 straight games.
In 1960, he took a job at Davidson, which was coming off an 11th consecutive losing season. He went 9-14 in his debut, one of only two times over an entire season in which he would finish with a losing record as a college coach.
Driesell won three Southern Conference tournaments and five regular-season championships at Davidson over nine years and went 176-65 before being hired at Maryland. He won 348 games with the Terrapins, a long-lasting school record that was finally broken in 2006 by Gary Williams.
Williams won the NCAA title in 2002. When he got home, a note from Driesell was waiting for him. It read: "Gary, YOU have made Maryland the UCLA of the East. Congratulations."
After leaving Maryland, Driesell was hired in 1988 by James Madison, a small Virginia school that finished 10-18 in 1987. He went 16-14 in his first year, 20-11 in his second season and led the Dukes to four straight NIT appearances before going to the NCAA Tournament in 1994.
Driesell compiled a 159-111 record at James Madison and enjoyed continued success at Georgia State. The Panthers were 29-5 in 2000-01 and upset Wisconsin in the opening round of the NCAA Tournament. Two years later, he retired in the early stages of his 41st season with a career record of 786-394. At the time, he ranked fourth in NCAA Division I wins, behind only Dean Smith, Adolph Rupp and Bob Knight.
Finally, at age 71, the man affectionately known by many as the Ol' Left-hander had enough.
"I'm just tired and I've got this bad cold and I'm just going to retire," Driesell said. "I'm looking forward to not having a job. I can get up when I want to and do what I want to."
Driesell is survived by four children. While at Duke, Driesell eloped with Joyce and got married in December 1952. She died in 2021.
The couple's only son, Chuck, played for the Terrapins under his father from 1981-85 and became an assistant to his father at James Madison. He was hired as the coach at The Citadel in 2010 and was fired after five losing seasons.
While helping his father at James Madison, Chuck Driesell learned the rigors of coaching.
"Dad gave me a lot of responsibility, and we worked hard," he said. "As a son and as a player, I'm not sure I understood how hard he worked. I figured it out pretty quickly."
