title: Mid-Shore trainers hit the seaside oval
author: TED BLACK tblack@somdnews.com
content:
Mid-Shore trainers hit the seaside oval

 July 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TED BLACK tblack@somdnews.com | Section: Sports 
 
 683
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A handful of owners and trainers with Mid-Shore connections made their way to Ocean Downs, a half-mile oval five miles west of Ocean City, but their ventures there were hardly for entertaining purposes or to savor the sand and sunshine.Last Wednesday, Ocean Downs hosted a quartet of $87,500 Maryland Sire Stakes finals for 3-year-olds of both gaits and genders on its annual "Summer Showdown" card for sophomore pacers and trotters. Several Mid-Shore owners, trainers and breeders performed well in those events as well as others on the card.
In the first parimutuel race on the card, trainer John Wagner of Centreville sent out a solid tandem that would garner second and fourth, respectively. Tony Babe (Jonathan Roberts) lived up to his billing as the 3-5 favorite to score in 1:55.4, while Wagner trainees Petes For Real (Fern Paquet Jr.) and Cloggs For Real (Corey Braden) finished second and fourth, respectively.
Then two races later in the $87,500 MDSS final for 3-year-old colt and gelding trotters, Wagner trainees Geralds A Keeper (Trae Porter) and K J Dash (Victor Kirby) finished one-two as expected. Geralds A Keeper lived up to his role as the 3-5 favorite when he overcame post six to gain command early to carve out all the fractions en route to a 1:58 score, his sixth in seven starts this year.
Then two races later in the $87,500 MDSS final for 3-year-old filly pacers, Yourgracefoundme (Eric Davis) finished second as an overlooked 36-1 shot as prohibitive 1-9 choice Fancy Like That (Johnathan Ahle) led throughout to prevail by seven lengths in 1:56 for owner-trainer Kasey Bendix. A sophomore daughter of Mr. Apples owned and bred by Jeffery Clark of Centreville, Yourgracefoundme sports a lifetime bankroll just shy of $100,000 from 21 starts.
Then just past the midway point of the Wednesday card, Sinatra De Vie (Ahle) lived up to his role as the 4-5 favorite in the $12,000 Open Handicap Trot when he overcame his assigned post eight and rallied from last year and widest of all down the backside and through the far turn en route to a three-length score in 1:55.1.
A 4-year-old son of Southwind Frank owned and trained by Eric Foster of Ridgely, Sinatra De Vie has won all four of his starts at Ocean Downs this summer and now sports eight wins and roughly $67,500 banked from 18 seasonal outings overall.
Several races later, Walden Woods (Hugh O'Neil) easily lived up to his billing as the even-money favorite in the $10,000 Open II class for older pacers when he gained command immediately from the coveted rail and led throughout en route to a three-length score while stopping the timer in 1:54.1. A 6-year-old Betting Line gelding owned and trained by Samuel "Wayne" Young of Church Hill, Walden Woods recorded his third straight score over the seaside oval.
Then one race later on the same card, Full Send (Russell Foster) easily lived up to his role as the even-money choice in a non-winners of $4,501 last four starts class for older pacers when he gained command through the clubhouse turn from the rail and led throughout en route to a three-length score in 1:52.4. A 7-year-old Western Ideal gelding trained by Eli Scott Jr. of Warwick, Full Send recorded his fifth win from 18 seasonal tries.
Last Thursday evening at Harrington Raceway, a half-mile harness racing oval in southern Delaware, Curtsyforpurrseco (Tim Tetrick) easily lived up to her role as the 3-5 favorite in the $110,000 Delaware Standardbred Breeders Fund final for 3-year-old filly pacers when she overcame post eight to gain command before the opener in 28.4, carved out honest fractions then drew clear late to a four-length score while stopping the timer in 1:56.1.
A sophomore daughter of Roddy's Bags Again trained by Jim King Jr. for owner Jo Ann Looney-King and bred by Winbak Farm in Chesapeake City, Curtsyforpurrseco completed a sweep of the DSBF spring series at Harrington and now owns five wins and just over $100,000 banked from 12 seasonal outings. She has also now won exactly one-half of her 22 career outings and boasts lifetime earnings just north of $200,000.

title: Going for the gold: Sudlersville Train Station Museum highlights local sports history
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Going for the gold: Sudlersville Train Station Museum highlights local sports history

 July 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: State News 
 
 455
 Words 

 Read News Document

 SUDLERSVILLE — Showcasing a small town with a rich history of esteemed sports, the Sudlersville Betterment Club presented exhibits of local renowned athletes at the Sudlersville Train Museum in July.Sudlersville Community Betterment Club showcased exhibits earlier this month featuring local sports heroes, according to club secretary Ginny Moran.
In addition to baseball Hall of Famer Jimmie Foxx, Sudlersville is also the claim to fame local home for extraordinaire Olympic archers, renowned skeet shooters, award-winning horse racing, championship golf, acclaimed target shooting and historic fox hunting.
Members Alison and Luke Howard, of the Wicomico Hunt Club, spoke on the activities of the only organized fox chase on the Eastern Shore.
The club hunts from Elkton, Maryland, to Bethel, Delaware. The fox chase has a prominent local history as the first fox hounds and foxes were brought to America in Queen Anne's County in 1650, she said.
The Wicomico Hunt Club houses all of their three breeds of hounds together at one kennel near Salisbury, she said.
Sudlersville is also home to several World Class Skeet Shooting Champions including Joseph M. George, who is entered into the Maryland Hall of Fame for Sports for 1,800 lifetime shooting wins. George's grandson, Jonathan Levan, is featured for his accomplishments winning Top Gun at the Grand National Waterfowl Hunt at the age of 17.
Greg Clark from the Sudlersville Skeet Club shared memories from pulling clay targets for the Club as a child.
A display of memorabilia showcased local sports champions Zach Schmidt and David Sink who were National Rifle Shooting Champions at national competitions and went all the way to Junior Olympics. Both participated in the Jacksonville State University Rifle Team in Alabama.
The event recognized former resident Jeff Hopkins for his World Championship of the Archery Shooters Association in 1997. Julie Russum, also from Sudlersville, was a state high school golf champion.
Humans aren't the only impressive athletes to come out of Sudlersville; Slick Tony, a Standardbred Pacer raised right out of Sudlersville was featured having 66 career wins to his credit.
Owner Nola Leager shared Slick Tony's pictures from the Dover, Harrington, and Ocean Downs Race Tracks, as well as recognitions from Hoof Beats Magazine.
Several local equestrians have been big winners in the Trotter and Acer Races and at one time Sudlersville was known as the "racingest town around," according to Moran.
With the mindset of "citizens serving citizens," since 1916, the Sudlersville Betterment Club is a group of volunteers who operate out of the Sudlersville Train Station Museum to collect, preserve, and maintain the history of Sudlersville and the surrounding community.
The Sudlersville Train Station Museum is located at the corner of Main St. and S. Linden St. and will be open during the Peach Festival Aug. 3.
More information about the museum can be found at sudlersvillemuseum.org.

title: Claxton, Blue notch top honors
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Claxton, Blue notch top honors

 July 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1264
 Words 

 Read News Document

 He's not a sprinter.And yet Tucker Claxton's speed is one of his better and perhaps most underrated qualities, especially when considering his shooting and passing skills.
"His speed is very deceptive," Kent Island High boys head lacrosse coach Bobby Woolley said of Claxton. "So when you think you're running with him, he's got another gear that he just quickly shifts into. And it doesn't matter if the teams put a (long) pole on him, or a shortie. It's just so difficult to defend him one on one. So that just allows a lot of guys to kind of free up, because in most cases he's getting a slide really early so it kind of allows things to get in motion for us."
Claxton seemingly put things in motion whenever he was on the field this season, pacing the Buccaneers to their ninth Bayside Conference championship in 12 years — excluding the COVID-canceled title games of 2020 and '21 — while leading the North Bayside in goals and assists en route to being named the North Bayside Offensive Player of the Year, as selected by division coaches.
"No one could stop him," Easton head coach Dennis Keenan said of Claxton, who netted 47 goals and 41 assists — both North Bayside highs — and 42 ground balls. "Watching film, I mean everybody knew what he was bringing to the table. But nobody could stop him."
The two-time defending Class 2A state champions, Claxton and the Buccaneers went 12-5 this season, earned their 11th division crown in 12 seasons — again excluding '20 and '21 — and weren't stopped until the 2A state semifinals, where the bid for a third consecutive state title was foiled by eventual state champion Glenelg.
And while he was the North's scoring leader, Claxton also proved to be a team leader, stepping into the void created by the graduation of Kasey Heath, Kent Island's outstanding goalie on the back-to-back state teams.
"I knew Tucker had the potential to be that guy," Woolley said of his senior midfielder who is headed to Mount St. Mary's. "Being around long enough you watch guys mature year over year, and I knew that he would come into his senior year just a different kid than he was in his junior year, where he didn't really have to have a voice. The fact that in his senior year he would, I knew he would respond well. He was certainly the guy that most guys turned to for the leadership that was needed."
Queen Anne's County turned and often got big plays when it needed them from senior goalie Dino Blue, named the North Bayside's Defensive Player of the Year.
"Phenomenal," Lions head coach Brad Niesz said of Blue. "This year he just settled in as the absolute backbone of our team. Was an absolute wall. Gave us transition opportunities that led to goals, led to opportunities, led to winning games."
Blue faced 172 shots this season, stopping 110 for a goals-against average of 6.8 per game and a save percentage of 64% for a Lions team that finished 7-6.
"He's just good," Woolley said of Blue, who does not plan on playing in the collegiate ranks. "He's spunky. He's twitchy. He's got great reflexes. I think he's able to position himself well against most of the common shots that are coming at him. You've got to get a little on top of him to get quality looks. I think he's a really athletic kid who has great stopping potential."
Woolley thought the Bucs had the potential for a third straight title run this past spring. Kent Island followed a familiar formula, playing stiff competition in the first half of the season in preparation for the playoffs. But that plan didn't produce the same results as in years past, as the Bucs struggled early.
"Normally we know who's going to emerge as the replacements for the guys we lose and this year just wasn't clearly defined going into the season," Woolley said. "So we had to use the first part of the year to kind of move pieces around and kind of figure out the puzzle that worked for us. The biggest challenge was finally finding the equation that worked for us via personnel. And along the way there was just some unusual hiccups. We were putting guys in positions to potentially fail as a result of us trying to see if they were the guy."
After a 1-3 start, the Bucs figured out who was best where, winning 11 of their final 13 games, earning Woolley all-North Coach-of-the-Year honors.
Here's a look at this year's all-North teams as selected by the coaches:
First TeamAttackDrew Schmidt, Sr., Easton: Helped Warriors to an 11-3 record and was second only to Claxton in total points, leading Easton with 54. Ranked second in goals scored for Easton (34) and shared the team lead for assists (20) with Hudson Royer. Is headed to Lynchburg (Virginia) University.
Owen Wynot, Sr., Kent Island: The Bucs' second-leading goal scorer with 32, Wynot also had six assists. Plans to continue playing at St. Mary's College.
Tyler Rardin, Sr., Easton: Led the Warriors with 35 goals and set up 15 more. Plans to walk-on at Salisbury University.
Micah Quinn, Sr., Kent Island: Another key cog in the Bucs' bid for a third straight title, Quinn totaled 30 goals and 10 assists. Headed to Flagler (Florida) College.
MidfieldHudson Royer, Sr., Easton: Keenan and the Warriors are probably still thinking of what might have been had Royer not suffered a game-ending injury against Kent Island during a 12-11 loss in the 2A East Region I final. Ended the season with 23 goals and 20 assists. Will join Schmidt at Lynchburg.
Keegan Green, Jr., Kent Island: Developed into another solid scoring option in a multi-headed offense. Green finished as the Bucs' second leading scorer, netting 28 goals and 16 assists (44 points).
Ryan Lee, Jr., Queen Anne's: Long-stick midfielder often drew the opposition's top scoring threat, and finished the season with 27 ground balls and 12 takeaways.
DefenseGavan Henry, Jr., Kent Island: The Bucs' top defender, Henry could play a shut down role and also direct as the defense developed through the season. Finished with three goals and three assists, but was a magnet for ground balls, totaling 55. Also caused 17 turnovers.
Colin Scattergood, Sr., Queen Anne's: Niesz called Scattergood a Swiss Army Knife for his ability to play anywhere on the defensive end. Finished the season with 46 ground balls, 14 takeaways, and scored a goal. Intends to play at Washington College.
Kyle Dyott, Sr., Easton: Dyott's communication skills and tenacity made him one the North's top defenders. "He was relentless on ball carriers," Keenan said of the senior defender who is headed to Emory and Henry College in Virginia.
Billy Schindler, Sr., Queen Anne's: After leaving lacrosse to focus on soccer, Schinder returned his sophomore year, and this season proved to be one of the division's top defenders. The short-stick defensive midfielder who is headed to Washington College to play soccer and lacrosse, finished with 44 ground balls and seven takeaways.
Face-off SpecialistQuinn McFaden, Sr., Kent Island: McFadden became a catalyst for the Bucs attack, winning 132 of 202 face-offs for a 65.3 percentage. Also collected 33 ground balls.
SECOND TEAMAttack: Will Speakman, Sr. Kent County; Jamison Kendall, So., Queen Anne's; Jackson Shiley, So., Queen Anne's; Jameson Krukiel, Sr., Queen Anne's; Midfield: Martin Parish, Sr., Kent County; Ethan Clark, Jr., Kent County; Landon Wallace, Sr., Kent County; Ethan Finlay, Jr., Easton; Defense: Frank Kelly, Sr., Queen Anne's; Ben Loller, Sr., Kent County; Ryan Myers, Sr., Kent County; Ty Finlay, Sr., Easton; Goalie: Jack Kilbourne, Sr., Easton; Faceoff: Owen Boeshore, Sr., Queen Anne's.

title: DURRIE'S DEDICATION
author: Bill Haufe
content:
DURRIE'S DEDICATION

 July 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 831
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The late Durrie Hayes would have enjoyed the afternoon of May 28, 2024, his light mustache unable to conceal that Cheshire cat-like smile.A large collection of friends, former players and assistants gathered in a loose, elongated semicircle inside the right-field foul line at Easton High's softball field on that spring day fit for a doubleheader.
Soon bats would be swung, pitches hummed, ground and fly balls collected, and runs scored as part of the school's inaugural alumni softball game.
Not everyone had come to play, but all had come to catch the pregame that featured speeches thick on compliments, and the unveiling of the newly erected scoreboard behind the center-field fence in Hayes' honor. And those who knew him well can pretty much imagine Hayes' reaction once his eyes settled on his name emblazoned across the top of the scoreboard in big, bold orange letters outlined in white on a black background.
"I can just picture him smiling that little smile he had," said Casey (Dulin) Baynard, a star on Hayes' early teams and now a Warrior assistant. "I think he would have been very proud."
Dr. Ed Baker, the longtime umpiring legend who said, "Hayes was by far the best softball coach that I every umpired a game for," agreed.
"Durrie was a very humble person," Baker said of Hayes, who died April 2, 2020 at age 70 after a brief battle with cancer. "Naturally he would be very, very pleased and honored to see such a scoreboard. But he was never looking for his name to be in flashing lights."
Jay Cappa, an assistant during Hayes' 13 years at Easton, perhaps pegged the former head coach's reaction best.
"He would have said, 'Who'd a thunk it?'" Cappa said. "I do believe he would have said, 'Who'd a thunk it?'"
Actually, it was Byrd Dog Wheeler who first thunk Hayes be memorialized, initiating the drive for a scoreboard honoring the school's Hall of Fame coach four years ago.
"It's incredible what that guy did," said Wheeler, another longtime friend and one of the ceremony's speakers. "And that one run he had there; what the last eight years? Jeez Louise."
Hayes coached the Warriors from 1995-2007, compiling an impressive 232-46 record that included seven Bayside Conference championships, six regional titles and three state championships. Wedged in that 13-year stretch was an eight-year run (2000-07), where the Warriors went 162-18 that included a 23-0 season in 2004 — an unbeaten streak that was extended to 30 games the following year — three state championships and three state runner-up finishes.
"He put in all that time going to Little League girls softball games and travel team softball games, and talking to the parents and getting them involved, and getting them to buy into the program at such a young age," Wheeler said. "By the time they got up to ninth grade they were on track and knowing what to expect and ready to play. No one else did anything like that.
"One thing he couldn't say is that, 'There's others out there that deserve that a lot more than I do.' Not a chance he could say that," Wheeler added.
Well, now hold on there big dog.
There was in fact somebody who would have penciled himself into the leadoff spot to protest that very point — Hayes.
"It was always about the girls," Wheeler conceded. "It wasn't about Durrie Hayes."
Others could easily see Hayes lobbying for his players' names to be adorned atop the scoreboard, instead of his.
"I think deep down he would have been very honored," longtime friend Debbie Urry said. "But I think he would have been embarrassed because it should have gone to the girls. He was always about the girls. He never wanted that kind of attention. I think he would have been very humbled and surprised. And he would have given credit to all the girls he ever coached."
Jay Chance, who coached with Hayes at Easton and Chesapeake College, watched the skipper consistently direct praise his players' way.
"He never really made it all about him," said Chance, who presented Hayes during the induction ceremony for Easton High's inaugural Athletic Hall of Fame class in September 2019. "It was more important to make a difference in the girls' lives than it was to win a game. That's what I liked so much about him. Although on game day you would never know that [laughing]. On game day it was about winning."
Oh, and the fun Hayes would have had filling out the lineups for both teams in the alumni game.
"He definitely would have loved the alumni game that we had after that," Baynard said.
As the ceremony wrapped up, Cappa and Chance reminisced and joked about what Hayes' take would have been on this big to-do.
"Jay said, 'Watch it. He's libel to send down a lightning bolt,'" Cappa said laughing. "I told Jay, 'He's not going to do it 'cause they're going to play a softball game. He ain't going to ruin the softball game.' He said, 'Yeah, I guess you're right.'"

title: Jackson finds Ravens to be perfect fit
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Jackson finds Ravens to be perfect fit

 July 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 551
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OWINGS MILLS — The Baltimore Ravens have shown they can make productive additions late in the offseason.No wonder hopes are so high for Eddie Jackson, the veteran safety they signed in the past few days.
"We seem to do this all the time, just get these vets that come here and do so much for us during the season," All-Pro safety Kyle Hamilton said Tuesday. "It's going to be so big for us to have him as part of the team."
Last year the Ravens added Jadeveon Clowney in August and Kyle Van Noy in late September, and those two combined for 18 1/2 sacks. In 2021, Baltimore signed Justin Houston around the start of training camp, and he gave the Ravens 14 sacks over the next two seasons. Now the 30-year-old Jackson arrives after seven years with the Chicago Bears.
"It just felt like a perfect fit," Jackson said. "Just knowing what they have in this building and the tradition of things, I just knew it (was) a perfect fit for me to come in and compete and do what I (have) to do to help the team get better and hopefully win the Super Bowl."
Jackson was an All-Pro in 2018 and made the Pro Bowl that season and the following one. He's one of three defensive backs to produce double-digit interceptions (15) and forced fumbles (10) since 2017, the year he entered the league. The other two are current Ravens cornerback Marlon Humphrey and ex-Baltimore cornerback Marcus Peters.
Jackson and Humphrey played together at Alabama. And Jackson is from South Florida and said he grew up about 15 minutes from Baltimore's other Jackson — star quarterback Lamar.
"Basically call him my cousin because (we're) both Jacksons," Eddie Jackson said. "To be on the same team as him is like one of those type of feelings. Just seeing what he brings to this game, to this league. Just how he (is) himself all of the time. And just how everyone rallies around him is special."
Eddie Jackson has also played with Ravens linebacker Roquan Smith when they were in Chicago. He knows running back Derrick Henry from college, as well as receiver Zay Flowers and cornerback Trayvon Mullen, who are from Florida.
"It seems like we've got a really Florida team, so he'll really fit right in," Humphrey said. "I loved Eddie when I played with him at Bama. Obviously he's a ball hawk — already had a pick-6 I think yesterday."
Lamar Jackson (illness) has been absent from practice this week, but the Ravens are otherwise pretty healthy. Jackson joins the defensive backfield after the offseason departure of Geno Stone, who had a team-high seven interceptions last season.
"I'm very excited to bring in Eddie Jackson," coach John Harbaugh said. "I remember him running to the ball for Alabama when we're looking at the draft and having all of these good years in Chicago (and) playing against him."
Notes: Humphrey said he slimmed down a bit for this season. He's around 190 pounds after playing the past couple seasons around 200. ... Harbaugh said T Daniel Faalele will get a look at guard. The Ravens lost three starters on their offensive line and there's now competition for those spots. ... Harbaugh on Lamar Jackson's return: "It's just a matter of when the doctors are going to clear him."

title: James saves U.S. from big upset
author: Bill Haufe
content:
James saves U.S. from big upset

 July 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: News 
 
 831
 Words 

 Read News Document

 LeBron James saved the U.S. from what would have been a stunning loss.James' layup with 8 seconds left was the go-ahead basket Saturday, and the U.S. Olympic team that'll soon head to the Paris Games escaped with a 101-100 win over South Sudan in London, rallying from a 16-point deficit to avoid perhaps the biggest upset in the program's history.
South Sudan, the African nation that gained its independence just 13 years ago and is about to play in the Olympics for the first time, led for more than half the game and had a chance to win at the end. But Carlik Jones' runner off the glass missed with about 4 seconds left, and the Americans survived.
"I'm going to be honest: I like those better than the blowouts," James said as he walked off the court. "At least we get tested."
Oh, they got tested — by a team that came into the game as 43.5-point underdogs , according to BetMGM Sportsbook.
"A good reminder that when we play against teams, it's the biggest game of their lives," U.S. coach Steve Kerr said. "We have to expect everyone to play like that."
Down by 16 at one point, the Americans dug out of that hole with an 18-0 run in the second half — then needed heroics at the end anyway. JT Thor's 3-pointer with 20 seconds left gave South Sudan a 100-99 lead, then the Americans called timeout and put the ball in James' hands.
He made it look easy: He waited, waited, waited, then drove and laid it in with ease to put the U.S. back on top, and the Americans got the stop they needed at the end.
James finished with a game-high 25 points, six rebounds and seven assists for the U.S., which improved to 4-0 with one game left — Monday vs. World Cup champion Germany — on its pre-Olympic exhibition tour. Anthony Davis added 15 points and 11 rebounds for the Americans.
Marial Shayok had 24 points for South Sudan and Jones had a triple-double — 15 points, 11 rebounds and 11 assists.
The teams will meet in group play in the Paris Olympics on July 31.
"It's basketball. It happens," U.S. guard Stephen Curry said. "You want to play perfect every game; it doesn't happen. But can you dig deep and do the little things that help you win? Offense can come and go, but defense is the thing that helps you win championships, medals, all that stuff."
It should have been a mismatch, and for the first half, it was — just not in the way anyone would have expected.
The U.S. roster has 12 players, all of them All-Stars or NBA champions or both, with a total of 189,038 points in their regular-season careers, with 7,832 combined starts. South Sudan has four players who have appeared in an NBA game. They've scored a combined 1,228 points and started 19 games.
Didn't matter. It was 8-0 U.S. after 2 1/2 minutes. The rest of the half: South Sudan 58, U.S. 34. The Americans allowed South Sudan to shoot 61% in the first half and got outscored 21-3 from 3-point range in the first 20 minutes.
"I did not do a great job preparing our team," Kerr said. "We did not focus enough on what they're capable of, and that's on me. I think that really allowed South Sudan to gain confidence early. ... They were great. They played a wonderful game and the ending was good for us, just to feel that, to feel what it's going to be like in Paris and Lille."
An 18-0 run in the second half — James involved in most of it — was what really saved the U.S., turning a 76-65 deficit into an 83-76 lead.
South Sudan led by 16 late in the first half — 58-42 — before the Americans got the last basket to cut the deficit to 14 at the break.
But the 18-0 run was key. James had four assists during the spurt and Curry, from about 35 feet, connected on a 3-pointer late in the third that gave the U.S. its first lead since the first quarter at 79-76.
Wenyen Gabriel banked in a 3-pointer to get South Sudan within 85-84, but James — his former teammate with the Los Angeles Lakers — connected on a 3 on the ensuing U.S. possession, and the Americans would eventually pull through by the slimmest of margins.
"Today we were able to represent our country with pride and we put up a good fight and showed the potential of our country," Gabriel said. "I think it was a proud moment for a lot of people."
Davis said the team got to the arena late, thrown off by standstill London traffic, and that routines going into the game were disrupted. Maybe so, but South Sudan showed the U.S. that nobody at the Olympics will concede anything to the four-time defending gold medalists.
"Doesn't matter when it comes to how close the game is," James said. "We went out there to get better."

title: Burnham has new title, old approach
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Burnham has new title, old approach

 July 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 800
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Rob Burnham's title has changed, not his approach."I'm competitive to a fault maybe," Burnham said. "I will lose sleep to prepare for a game. I will stress and wake up at three in the morning and go draw stuff on the board; paper, pad at the computer. Watch film and do all those things.
"But I did all those things before I was a head coach," Burnham continued. "So that's not new for me. The only thing that's new for me is there's a fancy title in front of my name."
That title is head football coach at Cambridge-South Dorchester High.
"Super excited," said Burnham, who was announced as the Vikings' new head coach earlier this month. "It's been a long time coming. Excited for the opportunity to be head coach for sure.
"I just like working with kids," the 45-year-old Burnham added. "I like taking a kid and giving him an opportunity to make himself better through athletics."
Though he was a head wrestling coach for two years at William Fleming High in Roanoke, Virginia, this is Burnham's first head coaching job in football.
He succeeds Toby Peer, who coached Cambridge-SD the past three seasons, compiling an 18-14 record, which included reaching last year's Class 1A state semifinals, where the Vikings lost to eventual state champion Fort Hill.
Burnham said Peer has retired from education and is now working for Altec Industries selling trucks.
"I didn't think he'd step away early. But that's what he decided to do," Burnham said of Peer.
Burnham, who has coached high school football for 25 seasons, began working with Peer at William Fleming. When Peer accepted the head coaching job at South Hagerstown he brought Burnham with him as offensive line coach and offensive coordinator. Together they helped the Rebels go 57-25 during Peer's eight years as head coach, and watched running back Isiaha Smith set the state single-season rushing record with 2,918 yards in 2013.
Peer stepped away as head coach at South Hagerstown when he became the school's athletic director. But he returned to the coaching ranks in 2021, when he took over at Cambridge-SD. Again, he brought his offensive line coach and OC with him.
A native of Kalamazoo, Michigan who played left tackle in high school before heading off to Western Michigan University, Burnham will continue handling the offensive and defensive lines despite his new title. He said he isn't sure if he will be offensive coordinator, but knows for certain he wants to run the football.
"We want guys to get out and attack downfield and run the football effectively at every turn," Burnham said. "As an offensive line guy, if I can run the ball every single play and win I'm good with that. Nobody wants to come and watch that, but I'm over it already. If we win the game we win the game. I throw it three times and we win, I'm good with it. I throw it 50 times and we lose I'm not good with it."
Burnham taught eighth grade math for two years at Mace's Lane in Cambridge before accepting a special education position at Cambridge-SD last year.
"Most of the kids in this building I know," Burnham said. "I either had them in class or they knew who I was from being over at Mace's Lane."
The Vikings lost only five players from last year's 9-3 team, including starting quarterback Blake LaBelle, now at Frostburg State University. The fact that the bulk of last year's Class 1A East championship team is back should help, especially on the defensive side, where Burnham plans to change little.
"Defensively, we're probably going to be almost identical because I think our kids played well to the 3-4 scheme with the two high safeties," Burnham said. "Our kids run fast enough to keep everything in front of us. And it's not a bend-but-don't-break philosophy, but it's more of a we're going to give you a little bit and then take away what you try to get, if that makes sense. We run well enough at every position defensively that we're going to be OK."
Cambridge-SD lost four coaches from last year's staff, but Burnham thinks he can handle that transition as well.
"I feel confident in my ability to assemble a staff that can put kids in a place to be successful in most situations," Burnham said. "There's a virtual guarantee that I'll encounter a situation that I haven't encountered before. But I have a number of people that I can call and talk to and get sound advice, people to bounce ideas off of if there's a situation I don't like."
At the top of Burnham's don't-like list is losing.
"I'm a bad loser. My wife said it's not one of my great qualities," Burnham said. "But I'm going to do things very, very similar to the way I've always done before."

title: SOARING TO GOLD
author: Bill Haufe
content:
SOARING TO GOLD

 July 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1048
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Aliah Raga has spent a lot of time airborne.She has worked on takeoffs and landings.
She has built speed then soared upwards as if ready to pierce the roof over her head. She has altered those trajectories with suddenness and grace, commanding her 5-foot frame into streamline flips and twists that are a mix between Simone Biles and Peter Pan.
She has come down only to go right back up, launching into a second high-flying, acrobatic arc that preferably ends with both feet planted firmly in one place, as she raises her arms and breaks into a glamorous smile.
Aliah Raga has spent a lot of time honing, polishing and perfecting the components of the double mini trampoline.
A lot of time.
"I've been doing the sport for 11 years," said Raga, formerly of Denton. "It took a lot of practices. A lot of hard days. And a lot of falling."
So when 19-year-old Raga and her United States trampoline and tumbling teammates received late notification about a schedule change on Day 1 of the FIG World Cup in Coimbra, Portugal on July 6, they were left little time to stretch, warm up and mentally prepare prior to their first pass.
Raga was angry.
And that has often proved not to be a good thing for the competition.
"I was actually really angry," Raga said during a phone interview last week. "And for some reason, I don't know why, but I seem to do well when I'm angry, or I feel I have something to prove."
Raga harnessed her anger enough to get through that first day, then came back the following day to post the competition's highest score en route to winning the gold medal in the women's double mini trampoline for her first international championship.
"Definitely," Raga said when asked if she surprised herself. "Honestly, I was just going to land two passes, have fun, and try my best to represent my country."
Fun.
Raga has had a lot of fun since beginning her gymnastics journey at Joan Dyott's Chesapeake Gymnastics in Easton when she was just two years old. She progressed from Dyott's "Tumble Bunnies" to elite status between ages 11 and 12, and eventually outgrew the Easton gym.
Homeschooled, she began making the trek from Denton to the Dulles Gymnastics Academy in Sterling, Virginia three times a week. She continued competing in artistic gymnastics — which includes vault, uneven bars, balance beam and floor exercise — and trampoline. But when she was 12, Raga was diagnosed with osteochondritis dissecans (OCD), a joint disorder in the elbow that can affect young gymnasts. She underwent surgery. When it was discovered the cartilage had become detached in her other elbow she again had surgery.
Despite those operations, Raga came back and qualified in the double mini for the world age group championships in Bulgaria just before her 13th birthday. Soon after, Raga's parents, Adrienne and Will Raga, conferenced with her coaches and decided instead of traveling to Virginia three times a week, Aliah would move in with a host family.
Raga shifted her focus solely to trampoline and tumbling after her elbow surgery. She continued to compete at a high level nationally and internationally, winning the USA Gymnastics championship on the double mini in 2021.
Progress was halted again in January 2023, when Raga tore three ligaments in her ankle during a practice. She avoided surgery, but was in a walking boot for weeks before going into physical therapy. Again she came back strong, winning her second national double mini title — just weeks after graduating from high school — before earning the silver medal at last year's world championships in Birmingham, England.
Raga won her third national championship in four years in Minneapolis last month.
With this being an Olympic year, there is no world championship in double mini, which is not an Olympic event. But Portugal hosted the World Cup, attracting 23 competitors from around the globe.
Then came Day 1's timing snafu.
"We didn't know they moved it up an hour," Raga said of the competition. "So when we went down there to change and get ready and warm up and stretch, (the other gymnasts) were already out on the floor getting their 15-minute warmup.
"So we had no warmup; no stretch," Raga continued. "We only took four turns before we had to salute and compete, which was honestly so stressful. Two of my teammates got injured because of it and couldn't compete their second pass because they were just so stressed."
Raga fumed, and winged her two passes in the preliminaries.
"I just took what I knew and I just did it," she said. "One of them wasn't the correct pass, but it still was enough to get me in the final in sixth place."
The top eight qualified for Sunday's Final 1 competition. And because the competition was broadcast on the Portuguese television, there would be no schedule mix-ups this time.
Each gymnast got one pass in Final 1, with the top four scores moving on to Final 2.
"When you do Final 1 and Final 2, you have to think strategically," Raga said. "Like most people will throw their harder difficulty pass first. But I know most of the girls. Their hardest difficulty is what I call my easier difficulty."
The double mini opens with a strong sprint onto the first small trampoline, where a gymnast launches upward for her first skill or aerial maneuver, lands, then launches into a second skill before a second landing.
On her Final 1 pass — which had a 7.2 degree of difficulty — Raga went through her two skills cleanly and stuck the landing for a score of 25.9, putting her in third place entering Final 2, where scores restart.
Spain's Melania Rodriguez led off Final 2. But the defending world champion, in a bid for the degree-of-difficulty record, over rotated while attempting a triple pike and rolled out on the landing. Portugal's Diana Gaga also went high risk, but couldn't complete her second skill.
Raga followed. She was again worked cleanly through her two skills. And though she took a step on her landing, her 8.4 degree of difficulty proved compensation enough to earn her a first-place mark of 26.8, giving her victory over runner-up Sienna Kuznak of Canada.
"I was nervous, but I prevailed," Raga said. "This is a really big deal for me and I'm very happy it turned out that way."

title: TOUGH ACT TO FOLLOW
author: Bill Haufe
content:
TOUGH ACT TO FOLLOW

 August 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1769
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Queen Anne's County High head field hockey coach Shana Corder already knows there will be no topping last year's near perfect run.All the Lions did in 2023 was win their first Bayside Conference championship in school history, and notch a program record 14 shutouts while yielding just two goals during a magical 15-1 season that ended with a 1-0 loss to Hereford in the Class 2A state semifinals.
"No topping that," Corder said. "The numbers were amazing."
And though Queen Anne's may not be as strong after graduating its entire starting defense from a year ago with the exception of goalie Cassidy Alexander, the Lions aren't likely ready to fall off the map.
"New team, new dream," Corder said. "They know we lost our entire defense, so it's the next man up; fighting for your spots. It's pretty much what we've been telling them. 'Be ready to be a team player. And this might have been your position last year but we need help in this position and you're good here and you're going to go there.'"
Kent Island again looks to be in a position to challenge for its 11th North Bayside title in 14 seasons — excluding the COVID-canceled 2020 championship game.
"It's the most balanced team I've had in my four years as head coach," Kent Island's Laura Harding said.
And should the Bucs stumble, Easton may be in line for its first division crown since 2010.
"This is probably the most athletic group of girls I've had the pleasure of coaching as a whole," Warrior head coach Kim Neff said.
While Kent Island, Easton and Queen Anne's figure to duke it out for top billing in the North Bayside, Debbie McQuaid will look to steer Saints Peter and Paul to a fourth Eastern Shore Independent Athletic Conference championship in five years.
"I'm excited about the energy that the younger kids are bringing," said McQuaid, whose chief conference rival could again be Gunston, which has reached the ESIAC final the past two years. "We've got some versatility so we'll be able to switch lines. That makes the coach happy."
Here's a look at this year's Mid-Shore teams.
EASTON
Head Coach: Kim Neff.
Who's Where: Goalie: Alli Newman (Sr.); Taylor Bowen (Fr.); Defense: Lea Boutte (Sr.); Kadence McGuckin (Jr.); Sammy Townsend (Jr.); Macy Graves (Fr.); Alden Gibbons-Neff (Fr.); Adeline Moore (So.); Midfield: Bis Johnson (Jr.); Myka Motovidlak (Sr.); Addison Knox (So.); Hannah Dahlen (So.); Stella Kabler (Jr.); Forwards: Maedy Leitzer (Sr.); Olivia Orrell (Sr.); Georgia Spies (So.); Ryann Quicke (So.); McKenna Clow (So.); Sutherland Chandler (Fr.).
Outlook: Neff would like to avoid a repeat of a year ago, when the Warriors opened with four consecutive overtime games. She also hopes to find replacements for graduated all-North Bayside first-team picks Emily Branic, Sydney Johnson and Jordan Reagan, but has been encouraged by what she's seen this preseason, which included a play-day win over perennial 1A power Pocomoke.
"This is not a rebuild," said Neff, who returns first-team picks Orrell and McGuckin. "They're just very fast, and they have really good foundational skills. I have high expectations for them, and a lot of them have played together because of travel ball. They really are a cohesive group. We're kind of moving forward from where we left off last year."
KENT COUNTY
Head Coach: Suzie Wright-Taylor.
Who's Where: Goalie: Abigail Strayer (Fr.); Defense: Taylor Strong (So.); Hailey Myers (Jr.); Tess Fuchs (Jr.); Midfield: Abby Gallo (Fr.); Liza Loller (So.); Mali Wirth (Fr.); Forwards: Kate Cannon (Sr.); Grace Gerstung (Jr.); Clare Gerstung (Fr.); McKenna Messik (Jr.); Amaya Spicer (Sr.); Nevaeh Blackiston (Fr.); Mackenzie Walker (Fr.).
Outlook: The Trojans were winless a year ago with one of the smallest teams Wright-Taylor has ever had under her direction, but there have been positive signs this preseason.
"The freshmen that have come in have played rec," said Wright-Taylor, who has often watched players coming through the county's youth program go to other schools. "They have some experience at least, so we're not starting totally from ground zero.
"For the most part that group played together at rec with that goalie," Wright-Taylor said of her six freshmen, which are led by Gallo.
Bolstering hopes are the return of Cannon, Fuchs, Strong, Loller, Grace Gerstung and Messik. And there was Thursday's scrimmage against Bohemia Manor and North East.
"We scored more goals today than we did all last season," Wright-Taylor said.
KENT ISLAND
Head Coach: Laura Harding.
Who's Where: Goalie: Brynja Petursson (So.); Parissa Butler (Jr.); Defense: Sydney Riska (Sr.); Emma Wackowski (Jr.); Laura Peck (Jr.); Kai Moore (So.); Emma Fleshman (Sr.); Makenzie Guidry (Sr.); Midfield: Ella Napier (Jr.); Lilly Snyder (So.); Rita Yost (Jr.); Sadie Latchaw (Sr.); Sydney Cox (Sr.); Lyla Baily (Jr.); Caelan Green (Jr.); Elizabeth Talbott (Sr.); Forwards: Ellie Burnside (Sr.); Audrey Fleshman (So.); Caroline Levin (Sr.); Willow Yost (Jr.); Parker Tengwall (So.); Anna Fronczek (Jr.); Madison Jordan (Sr.).
Outlook: The Bucs went 8-6 a year ago, which included three straight one-goal losses to open the season and another against Queen Anne's in the 2A East Regional playoffs that ended it.
But Harding is excited by what she has seen this preseason.
"I don't have like a Megan Carpenter," Harding said of her former standout now playing at the University of Massachusetts. "I just have a full squad of girls that play field hockey year round. It's fun to watch."
The return of Riska, who did not play last year, strengthens the defense, while Burnside and the Yosts — all first-team North Bayside picks — provide a solid foundation which could be set for a series of title challenges.
"Talent across the board," Harding said. "I think we have a lot of depth. The kids coming off the bench are almost as strong as the kids starting on the field."
NORTH CAROLINE
Head Coach: Molly Elliott.
Who's Where: Goalie: Selena Lopez (Jr.); Alyssa Hand (Fr.); Defense: Brooklyn Spencer (Jr.); Abby Jones (Jr.); Emily Kimble (Sr.); Midfield: Morgan Knott (Sr.); Kylie Ogden (Jr.); Ashlynn Bisesi (So.); Reece Bisesi (Jr.); Forwards: Gracie Faulkner (Jr.); Jamie Robey (Fr.); Julia White (Fr.); Reagan Rizer (Jr.).
Outlook: After five years as Easton's junior varsity head coach, Elliott begins her third year with the Bulldogs, the last two as head coach.
And though North Caroline doesn't figure to challenge for a division title, Elliott has three players with club experience, including Knott, who has verbally committed to play at Central Michigan.
"We have a lot more experience on the field than we have had in seasons past," Elliott said. "We've been plagued the last few seasons by some major injuries So having Morgan and Ashlynn and Reece on the field at the same time isn't something we've been able to do in seasons past, and so I'm very excited that we have a very healthy starting midfield line.
QUEEN ANNE'S
Head Coach: Shana Corder.
Who's Where: Goalie: Cassidy Alexander (Sr.); Caroline Kimball (Jr.); Defense: Melanie Gill (Fr.); Midfield: Ava Fields (Sr.); Ellee McLean (Sr.); Haley Cole (Jr.); Jordan Bilbo (Jr.); Taylor Brown (So.); Ella Rebstock (So.); Forwards: Aly Edwards (Sr.); Jolie Leager (Sr.); Jamie Baldwin (Sr.).
Outlook: Like a number of coaches, Corder will shift players between lines, especially at midfield and forward.
But whereas the defense was last year's anchor, this season it will be the offense that needs to shoulder the load
"My defense carried us last year," said Corder, whose team didn't yield a goal until the final regular-season game against Stephen Decatur. "This year my message is offense needs to do the same until they can figure out their way and our strategy on defense."
While Corder is mixing a new lineup to replace first-team all-North defenders Abbie Denes — now at St. Mary's — Julia Reburn and Molly Holthaus, and well as North Bayside player of the year Faith Novak and first-team forward Gabrielle Scully, there is talent up front.
Corder said she will lean on Cole, who is headed to James Madison at the midfield. Bilbo, who had a knack for big goals a year ago, is also back. Fields and McLean have started four years, giving Queen Anne's one of the strongest midfields in the Bayside.
"It's going to be a different year this year for Queen Anne's field hockey," Corder said. "We're going to rebuild, but it's totally fine."
ST. MICHAELS
Head Coach: Karen Hopkins.
Who's Where: Goalie: Olivia Patrick (Jr.); Defense: Brynn Lizewski (Sr.); Phoebe Cole (Sr.); Regan Wibberley (Jr.); Rebeca Martinez (Jr.); Midfield: Jordyn Beckett (So.); Stella Wibberley (Fr.); Kim Montoya-Guzman (Fr.); Midfield: Molly Genrich (Sr.); Maddie Dunker (Sr.); Tess Weller (Jr.); Forwards: Karina Mazur (Sr.); Abbie Fisher (So.); Ella Marr (Fr.); Penny Turner (Fr.); Zoe Cerrato (Fr.); Kayla Montoya-Guzman (Jr.).
Outlook: Returning first-team midfielders Dunker and Genrich, and forward Mazur give the Saints a nice base to work off. The defense returns plenty of experience, and generating more offense will be among the top priorities.
"The leadership we have through our five seniors is very apparent," Hopkins said. "They've been helping the younger girls as well as leveling up their play. We have such positive energy on the field. We're striving for the intensity. We are striving for better plays and more strategy and more consistency."
SAINTS PETER & PAUL
Head Coach: Debbie McQuaid.
Who's Where: Goalie: Pyper Mister (Fr.); Rynn Morgan (So.); Defense: Kat Murphy (Sr.); Reagan Wolters (Fr.); McKenzie Foster (So.); Lucy Rankin (Jr.); Midfield: Claire Beiber (Sr.); Sadie Jacobs (Fr.); Angie Webb (So.); Forwards: Jules Stepp (Jr.); CC O'Connor (Sr.).
Outlook: The Sabres lost a number of key players from last year's 14-2 title-winning team, including ESIAC player of the year Gennie Webb — now at Virginia Commonwealth — Morgan Quade, Emmary Sweeney, Cadence Kelley and Schuyler Gary.
The cupboard is hardly bare though.
Angie Webb returns at the midfield and is joined by St. Michaels transfer Beiber, who is headed to VCU. The front line also looks strong with Stepp and O'Connor returning.
"I usually get some really good athletes, but they're not always field hockey players," McQuaid said. "This year I've got a good bunch of athletes who are actually field hockey players."
GUNSTON
Head Coach: Yvonne Gazelle.
Who's Where: Goalie: Lorelei DeGour (Fr.); Defense: Izzy Labrador (Fr.); Victoria MacGlashan (Sr.); Lila McDermott (Fr.); Midfield: Layla Kent (Jr.); Genevieve Baughman (Jr.); Camilla Nonemaker (So.); Forwards: Grace Shepherd (Sr.); Gabi Shepherd (So.); Kate Zottarelli (So.); Tori Nessly (Sr.).
Outlook: Sophia Kent, a four-year fixture in goal, has graduated and is now at St. Mary's. The Herons have made it to the ESIAC championship the past two years, but Gazelle thinks it will be a year of trying to find the right combinations in hopes of making a third straight conference final.
"It's going to be a building year," Gazelle said. "We're all pretty new. We have some brand new ones to the sport, but there's a lot of promise."
Layla Kent provides a building block at midfield, while Grace Shepherd figures to be a force up front.

"This is not a rebuild," said Neff, who returns first-team picks Orrell and McGuckin. "They're just very fast, and they have really good foundational skills. I have high expectations for them, and a lot of them have played together because of travel ball. They really are a cohesive group. We're kind of moving forward from where we left off last year."
KENT COUNTY

Outlook: The Trojans were winless a year ago with one of the smallest teams Wright-Taylor has ever had under her direction, but there have been positive signs this preseason.
"The freshmen that have come in have played rec," said Wright-Taylor, who has often watched players coming through the county's youth program go to other schools. "They have some experience at least, so we're not starting totally from ground zero.
"For the most part that group played together at rec with that goalie," Wright-Taylor said of her six freshmen, which are led by Gallo.
Bolstering hopes are the return of Cannon, Fuchs, Strong, Loller, Grace Gerstung and Messik. And there was Thursday's scrimmage against Bohemia Manor and North East.
"We scored more goals today than we did all last season," Wright-Taylor said.

Outlook: The Bucs went 8-6 a year ago, which included three straight one-goal losses to open the season and another against Queen Anne's in the 2A East Regional playoffs that ended it.
But Harding is excited by what she has seen this preseason.

The return of Riska, who did not play last year, strengthens the defense, while Burnside and the Yosts — all first-team North Bayside picks — provide a solid foundation which could be set for a series of title challenges.

And though North Caroline doesn't figure to challenge for a division title, Elliott has three players with club experience, including Knott, who has verbally committed to play at Central Michigan.
"We have a lot more experience on the field than we have had in seasons past," Elliott said. "We've been plagued the last few seasons by some major injuries So having Morgan and Ashlynn and Reece on the field at the same time isn't something we've been able to do in seasons past, and so I'm very excited that we have a very healthy starting midfield line.

While Corder is mixing a new lineup to replace first-team all-North defenders Abbie Denes — now at St. Mary's — Julia Reburn and Molly Holthaus, and well as North Bayside player of the year Faith Novak and first-team forward Gabrielle Scully, there is talent up front.

title: BANKING ON EXPERIENCE
author: Bill Haufe
content:
BANKING ON EXPERIENCE

 August 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 737
 Words 

 Read News Document

 AMERICAN CORNER — James Jackson isn't used to this.Seemingly everywhere Colonel Richardson High's head football coach looks this preseason there's a senior here and a senior there.
"I need to talk to (longtime assistant and former head coach) Neil Lambert, but I believe this is the biggest senior class Colonel football's ever had," Jackson said. "Under my supervision it's definitely the most."
And for that reason optimism is high for a group that would like to notch seven or eight regular-season victories and possibly match, or even exceed, the postseason run of the 2021 team that made a bunch of school history, which included reaching the Class 1A state quarterfinals for the first time.
"They're all talking about making a deep playoff run," Jackson said. "They're just looking forward to getting back to where we were their freshman year."
The Colonels look to have the talent and certainly the experience to make a push in that direction after going 4-6 a year ago, which included a 4-0 mark against Bayside 1A competition.
Seniors dominate both sides on the ball, with 6-foot-2, 195-pound quarterback Tarron Hammond directing the Double Wing T attack for a third straight year. Behind him are senior wingbacks Dylan Cecil (5-6, 140) and Eamare Jones (5-8, 155), senior fullback Collin Brewer (5-10, 200) and junior wingback Derrick Mitchell (5-11, 185), who led the Colonels in rushing a year ago. Junior wingback Bradley Thomas (5-9, 205) and senior fullback Chatydrick Pickrom (5-11, 230) could also be rotated into the backfield.
Senior tight ends Domnique Caven (6-0, 175) and Carter Turbitt (5-11, 180) provide two nice targets for Hammond, as well as additional push for the Colonels' steady-as-it-goes run game.
"I think clock control is always in our favor," Jackson said. "So running the football, trying to keep the ball in our possession as long as possible, wearing defenses down, that's what we're known for. If we can continue that, we have more success when we have the ball longer than our opponent."
Though Jackson has yet to settle on a starting right tackle, the remainder of the line is all seniors. Gavin Weiss (5-9, 230) is at center, with Chris Rockwell (5-10, 225) at right guard and Duilio Berduo-Morales (5-8, 235) at left guard. Stevens Austinville (6-3, 200) starts at left tackle.
"The seniors have been together for three years," Jackson said. "It's just now making it all come together."
What may help pull things together this season was what Jackson thought was missing in 2023 — senior leadership.
"We only had two seniors last year," Jackson said. "So this senior class now, none of them knew how to become a leader. I feel like now there's more talking in practice. There's quite a few of them trying to be leaders. So if we can get all the guys to follow behind these guys we should be pretty good."
The defense also has the potential to be pretty good.
Rockwell and Brewer, who shared the team lead in sacks last year with 10, line up at the ends, with Berduo-Morales at one tackle and Pickrom (8½ sacks), who can be a big-time difference maker, at the other tackle. If that group can tie up opposing linemen, inside linebackers Thomas and Cecil, and outside backers Mitchell, Jones and junior Carlens Jean Baptiste (5-6, 140) should be in position to make tackles.
Caven and Turbitt are back at the corners, while junior Jayquan Wilkins (5-7, 145) and sophomore JaZir Dickerson (6-0, 170) are the safeties.
"Coverages have got to get better, but in a week or two I think we'll be closer to where we need to be," Jackson said. "But we looked a lot better on our tackling in the scrimmage (against Sussex Tech) than we did all last season. Last season there was a lot of miss-tackles early. But in the scrimmage I thought with did a good job of gang tackling. And the first man to the ball was actually either holding on waiting for help, or making the tackle.
Since its history-making playoff run of 2021, Colonel — after taking a first-round forfeit over Washington in the 2022 playoffs — has been knocked out of the postseason by Bohemia Manor the last two years, including last year's 12-7 first-round loss.
"This group of starters haven't been past the first round of the playoffs," Jackson said. "They're looking for a deep playoff run this year. I feel coming in with experience, that hopefully will carry us to a good season."

title: TALL TASK
author: Bill Haufe
content:
TALL TASK

 August 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 642
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WORTON — Harold Somerville's biggest challenge heading into his third year as Kent County High's head football coach may not be figuring out who he's going to plug in at left tackle or outside linebacker.No, Somerville's biggest task may be simply getting his players to believe in themselves.
"The talent's there," Somerville said after Saturday morning's scrimmage against North East of Cecil County. "They got to believe it."
Somerville isn't saying the Trojans are going to compete for titles or make a deep playoff run. But in Saturday's scrimmage against North East there were plenty of encouraging signs.
Terrell Fennell slipped around left end, found an open sideline and blazed about 40 yards for a touchdown. There were a handful of other big-chunk plays, and the defense showed solid pursuit to the ball and gang tackled.
Somerville can also drop back to late last season in terms of his team's growth. One week after getting routed by Snow Hill 47-6 in their regular-season finale, the Trojans upended the Eagles, 34-18, in the first round of the Class 1A East Region playoffs.
"We're not looking bad," Somerville said. "I was pleased with Saturday. We know we've got some work to do, but I was pleased with it."
The offensive line lost two starters from last year's 2-9 squad, and that's where the most work may be needed in terms of getting stronger.
Sophomore Taeshaun Demby (6-foot-1, 250 pounds) starts at center, and is flanked by senior right guard Harrison Gibby (6-0, 190) and sophomore left guard Andrew Fennell (5-9, 200). Senior Wyatt Toulson (5-10, 180) starts at left tackle, while senior Wesley Townsend (6-4, 315) is at right tackle.
"I think we can compete with the other 1A schools," Somerville said of Bayside rivals Cambridge-South Dorchester, Colonel Richardson, Snow Hill and Washington. "I honestly feel as though if our line just gives the quarterback enough time to get the ball off I think that we can really compete. And I feel real comfortable with our receivers and our running backs."
He should considering most every one of them returns from last year.
Sophomore Dwan Harris (6-1, 170) is back at quarterback and looks to have a solid cast of backs that include senior Terrell Fennell (5-7, 150), juniors Scottie Ford (5-9, 140) and Tyrel Dean (5-8, 165), and sophomore Kalief Roberts (5-9, 150).
The receiving corps also looks strong, led by senior Jonah Somerville (5-7, 152) — the coach's son — who can line up in the slot or wide, as well as at quarterback or in the backfield. Harris' other two wide targets are sophomore Dylan Hurtt (5-8, 130) and Ramon Peterson (5-9, 150), while seniors Jysir Valentine (6-4, 240) and Shakur Wilson (6-1, 180) are at tight end.
Defensively, Kent will go with either a 4-3 or 5-3 scheme, with Andrew Fennell and Townsend at the tackles, and Toulson at nose, depending on the lineup. Valentine and Wilson will be the ends.
Coach Somerville admitted his linebacking unit struggled some against North East, but part of that was because Ford and Dean did not play. When it has a full complement of players, Kent will have junior Zayvion Brown (5-9, 160) and Ford as outside backers and Dean inside.
The secondary appears to be a strongpoint, with Terrell Fennell and Peterson at the corners, and Somerville and Roberts playing safety.
"I think our defense, at least in the second half, we were playing better than the offense," said Coach Somerville, who played nose tackle on Kent County's 1989 and '90 Class 1A state championship teams. "Especially our DBs. Our DBs are very experienced. They know how to read the ball."
Jonah Somerville will handled kickoffs and Harris will punt.
"I honestly believe, if they really believe in themselves and the jell together, that we can go to that next level and not just win two games like we have been the last couple years," Coach Somerville said.

title: Davis looks to build on Bucs' success
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Davis looks to build on Bucs' success

 August 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 854
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — Zach Davis has always been a builder."I was one of those guys, 'Oh, they went 0-10? Let me give a shot at that thing,'" Davis said. "That was kind of my thing."
As Kent Island High's new head football coach, Davis has been busy building relationships with coaches, players and the community since June. And though he looks to build another winning season, Davis knows he has taken over one of the Bayside Conference's better-built programs.
"I've been a program builder 'til here," Davis said prior to Thursday afternoon's practice. "I really want to see what we can do at a place that's been traditionally pretty good."
After three consecutive three-year stints at schools in West Virginia — Riverside, Nitro and most recently Buckhannon-Upshur — the 39-year-old Davis begins his 10th season as a head coach in a place that hasn't had a losing season since 2006.
"We've been coming to the Shore since 2008," said Davis, whose wife Emily (Gorin) is an Easton High graduate. "We've been trying to come back here. Had a couple of opportunities to come back, but they just didn't feel right. This one felt right.
"The thing about high school football is what works at one program can be different at another program," Davis added. "So when I come here, I have taken a lot of what Kent Island's been good at and just said, 'Hey, let's continue to do that.' My big thing is I try to remember the heartbeat."
Davis continues a family legacy of coaching. His grandfather was a coach, and his father, Storm Davis, who pitched for 13 seasons in the major leagues and was part of the 1983 World Series-winning Baltimore Orioles, coached football at Jacksonville Trinity Christian Academy in Jacksonville, Florida, where Zach was an all-state center.
"I got cut from my middle school baseball team in seventh grade," Zach Davis said. "That was the last time I played baseball. Kind of got to do my own thing."
Davis went to East Carolina before transferring to Liberty University, where he played every offensive line position at one point over three years, and started at left tackle in 2008, his senior year.
"I was in the film room all the time, which prepared me to be a coach," Davis said.
He got into the high school coaching ranks, spending three years at Riverside and three at Nitro before moving onto Buckhannon-Upshur, which is about the size of Kent Island, but played in the state's largest classification against schools from more urban areas like Morgantown and Charleston.
"We always improved it from what it was," Davis said of the programs he coached.
He now becomes only the fourth different head coach in the history of Kent Island's program, succeeding Bryon Sofinowski, who compiled a 118-64 record over 16 seasons (2001-2014, 2022-23), which included leading the Buccaneers to their first and only state championship appearance two years ago. Sofinowski retired after last season.
"I've got coach Sof's keys and I'm going to keep these," Davis said. "It says Sofinowski on it. It's a good reminder where we came from, where we want to go, and how we want to do it."
How the Bucs' new head coach wants to do it is similar to how his predecessor did it, though there may be a few new wrinkles.
"A lot of it is similar but some of the vernacular has changed," said Davis, who plans to keep it on the ground, but likes play action, and also has a two-minute spread package he can use. "Just trying to keep it as similar as possible. If that's what works here, it's good for us.
"As you can imagine, most people are like, 'Who is this guy?'" Davis continued. "I said, 'Guys, I'm here to assimilate into you and then just bring some new ideas. Not that it's better. Some of it's just different."
Senior quarterback Gavan Henry figures to help the transition process, though Kent Island graduated the bulk of its offense from a year ago, including its entire starting offensive line, backs Shane Bogardus and Austin Holland, and top receiving threats Tucker Claxton and Lloyd Price.
The defense also graduated big names, including Bayside Defensive Player of the Year Giuseppe Mellinger. While names will be different, what doesn't figure to change is the unit's base look, which is again under the direction of longtime defensive coordinator Tim Goodrich.
"He tells me all the time if I can score 14 points we'll win a lot of games," Davis said of Goodrich.
As for pressure, Davis said he doesn't feel any added weight taking over a winning program compared to those that struggled before he took the reins.
"I think every good coach should feel pressure," Davis said. "And that should come from yourself, that you're going to do it the best way you can do it. My big thing is win the day. I got that from (current UCLA head coach) Chip Kelly years ago when he was at Oregon. Just be better today than you were yesterday.
"I'm really looking forward to just being here and getting to know everybody, and trying to just keep this program going the way it has been," Davis said.

title: O'Connor's big day leads Easton
author: Bill Haufe
content:
O'Connor's big day leads Easton

 September 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 723
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The message didn't surface until after the game.Easton High head football coach Matt Griffith brought up that little note, saying how some Kent Island players had sent an Instagram screen shot to Warrior quarterback Mikey O'Connor earlier this week.
"They sent it to us," Griffith said. "It said, 'Come out and support Kent Island. It's Gavan (Henry), their quarterback, against Kevin's brother.'"
Well, Kevin O'Connor's younger brother had quite the night.
Mikey O'Connor rushed for a career-high 250 yards, including three touchdowns, and threw for 146 yards and a pair of TDs Friday, as Easton defeated Kent Island, 43-24, in a battle of Bayside Conference unbeatens.
"He's a really good player," Kent Island head coach Zach Davis said of Mikey O'Connor, the third O'Connor brother to play quarterback at Easton. "And they use him well; running and passing. He's a load."
O'Connor proved to be just that, scoring on runs of 5, 1 and 4 yards to help the Warriors (4-0) build a 21-10 halftime lead.
That lead stood until late in the third quarter, when Kent Island's Jaxon Hess raced 25 yards around right end for an apparent touchdown. But that score was erased when the Buccaneers (3-1) were called for holding. Four plays later, Kent Island punted the ball to the Easton 1.
The Warriors pieced together a 10-play, 99-yard drive that ended with O'Connor hitting Chase Raab for a 24-yard touchdown. Dominic Stanco's point-after boot made it 28-10 with 8:49 remaining in the game.
"That was huge," said Griffith of Kent Island having a score taken away before the Warriors lengthened their advantage to 18. "We talked about trying to finish. And I think that's the biggest thing. We've focused all week long on execution and finishing the game. And I thought tonight we did."
Kent Island came right back, as Henry hit Jackson Towers for a 64-yard touchdown pass that — together with Spencer Chappell's PAT — pulled the Bucs within 28-17 with 6 minutes left.
But Easton sealed the win when it scored two touchdowns in 58 seconds.
O'Connor found a wide-open Diontaye Copper for a 16-yard touchdown pass, then snagged a high snap from center and hit Raab with a two-point conversion pass for a 36-17 lead with 3:31 to go in the game. Kent Island fumbled on its next play from scrimmage, giving the Warriors possession at the Bucs' 27. Three plays later, Jordan Horsey bulled through the middle for an 11-yard touchdown with 2:23 remaining. Stanco's PAT made it 43-17.
"We gave up a late touchdown, but besides that, they only gave up three points in the first half," Griffith said of his defense. "The defense responded late in the second. That was key. Coming out in the third quarter and stopping them. Then we stalled and it was a defensive game most of the (scoreless) third quarter. Then we got back on track offensively and that's was good to see."
Easton drove 87 yards on its first possession to take a 7-0 lead on O'Connor's 5-yard touchdown run around left end.
The Warriors forced a Bucs' three-and-out, and had moved back into Kent Island territory, when Hess intercepted O'Connor in the left flat and sprinted 55 yards for a touchdown. Chappell's PAT forged a 7-7 tie with 5:40 left in the first quarter.
The game remained close. O'Connor scored on a 1-yard run, but Stanco's extra-point attempt was blocked, giving the Warriors a 13-7 lead with under 3 minutes left in the first quarter.
Kent Island shaved that lead to 13-10 just 53 seconds into the second quarter, when Chappell hammered a 38-yard field goal.
Easton responded with O'Connor's 4-yard touchdown run and a two-point pass to Colin Mooney for a 21-10 halftime lead.
"Good football team," Davis said of Easton. "Definitely a physical football team. We weren't as physical as we needed to be tonight. And we had some big plays taken away by penalties."
Henry fired his second touchdown pass with 43.2 seconds left in the game when he hit Isaiah Diaz for a 29-yard score.
"We've got work to do obviously," Davis said.
O'Connor said the same thing of Easton.
"I thought this win was big for us. Kind of a like statement," said O'Connor, who leads Easton into another battle of unbeatens next Friday at defending Class 2A state champion Stephen Decatur. "I feel like I played all right. But I could have done a lot of things better."

title: Yost's hat trick paces Bucs
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Yost's hat trick paces Bucs

 September 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 700
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — It took Kent Island High's field hockey team some time to adjust to life without graduated standout Megan Carpenter last year.Without Carpenter — who was seemingly everywhere on the field — the Bucs dropped their first three games, and were outscored 8-7 through their opening five games.
That has not been the case this season.
Kent Island showed its strength on offense, defense and at the midfield Thursday, as Willow Yost notched her first hat trick of the season and Ellie Burnside totaled three assists to fuel a 4-1 victory over Crisfield at Andy Schipul Stadium.
"We don't really have a superstar," Bucs head coach Laura Harding said after her team improved to 4-1. "We are a very, very balanced team. And I think last year we lost Megan and it took us a little while to figure it out because she did everything for us. She was on defense. She was on offense. She was distributing the ball all over the field. Everywhere.
"So it just took us a little while last year to figure it out, which is why I think we were way stronger at the end of the year," added Harding of a team that won eight of its last 11 games. "And we have a lot of girls on this team that play year round."
Harding may have felt she was watching last year's slow start during Thursday's first half, as the Buccaneers and Crabbers (3-2) were tied at 1-1.
"I just felt like we were a little flat in the first half and it just took us a while to get going," Harding said. "Yes, we have a very strong mid(field) and a very strong D. So that's nice. But then we just have to work on getting it in the cage, which we did the rest of the game. We were just flat in the beginning."
Yost gave Kent Island a 1-0 lead with 55 seconds remaining in the first quarter, when she scored off Sadie Latchaw's assist. Crisfield struggled to get the ball past Kent Island's midfield through the first quarter and into the second. But with 3:43 left in the half, Emily Engle set up Mya Pendry's tying goal off a corner.
"That was a beautiful goal that Crisfield had on that corner," Harding said. "The passing was gorgeous. So kudos to them."
Just a 1:20 later though, Parker Tengwall scored off the first of Burnside's three assists. Tengwall just missed giving Kent Island a two-goal halftime lead when she clanged a shot off the left post with less than a minute left in the half.
The Bucs had three corner opportunities to the Crabbers' two in the third quarter, before Burnside set up Yost's second goal for a 3-1 lead with 5:08 to go in the third.
"We kept turning over the ball and we kept passing it to the other team," Yost said of Kent Island's early struggles. "But then after the first half we definitely connected better."
The Burnside-to-Yost combination connected again with a little over 9 minutes remaining off a corner that widened Kent Island's cushion to 4-1.
"I definitely think her being in an offensive mid and me in the center, it works really well together," Yost said of her scoring connection with Burnside.
Yost thought there was a tendency for the Bucs to crowd one side of the field last season instead of spreading out. That appears to have been fixed this early season, as the Bucs have outscored their first five opponents, 13-3.
"I think we have a couple things to clean up," Harding said. "We've been working on both circles. Like I don't think that goal should have happened. And I don't the one against Parkside should have happened. So we have to work.
"But the middle of our field is solid," Harding continued. "We just have to work on finishing on the offensive end and not letting those goals in. But way better start than last year."

Haley Cole, Jamie Baldwin and Jolie Leager had one goal apiece for Queen Anne's (4-1) and Ava Fields had an assist.
